full_judgment:
"Let the records be called for and a Rule issue calling upon the opposite party No. 1 show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 14-3-1996 and 19-3-1996 respectively passed by Additional District Judge, Magura in Title Appeal No. 134 of 1991 dismissing the appeal and affirming those dated 15-6-1991 and 19-6-1991 respectively passed by in Title Suit No. 111 of 1989 decreeing the plaintiff suit should not be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper." 

 4. The defendant No.6 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint and stated inter alia that 8 decimals of land of suit plot No. 1093 out of 20 decimals, 5 decimals out of 32 decimals land of suit plot No. 1250, 10 decimals of land out of 60 decimals of land of suit plot No. 1786 and 7 decimals out of 44 decimals of non suit No. 116 and 7 decimals out of 41 decimals of land of non suit plot No. 117 belonged to Sudanya and, the father of the defendant No.6 purchased those lands by registered kabala dated 26-2-1953. 8 decimals of land out of plot No. 1093 acquired by WAPDA and the father of the defendant No.6 got compensation. The suit land has been correctly recorded in SA Khatian No. 1144. Kartik Chandra Biswas became owner by auction purchase in respect of 12 decimals of land of suit plot No. 1093 out of 21 decimals, 21 decimals out of 32 decimals of land of suit plot No. 1250 and 50 decimals out of 60 decimals of land of suit plot No. 1786 of the same was correctly recorded in SA Khatian No. 1143. Kartik Chandra Biswas sold land to Ataur Rahman by registered kabala deed 28-5-1969 and the father of the defendant No.6 being co- sharer filed preemption case in respect of the said kabala being Miscellaneous case No. 523 of 1970 which was allowed on contest. Said Ataur preferred Misc. Appeal No. 42 of 1975 and the said appeal was dismissed and preemption was confirmed. 

 7. The Trial Court upon considering the evidence on record and hearing the parties decreed the suit by judgment and decree dated 15-6-1991 and 19-6-1991 respectively. 

 10. Mr. AH Mahfoozur Rahman learned Advocate along with Mr. Mashiul Alam, Advocate appearing. on behalf of the defendant No.6 petitioner has taken me through the judgment of both the Courts and placed the evidence of both the parties and submitted that the Trial Court on both facts and law committed error of law in passing the impugned judgment discarding the Rule of evidence. The evidence of DWs 2, 3 and 4 were also misread by the Courts below and further failed to note that the plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of title and confirmation and possession over only 52 and 1/2 decimals of land but the plaintiff produced PWs. 2 and 3 to corroborate the evidence of PW.l but PW.2 and 3 being the witness of possession only prove the possession of 16 decimals of land out of the 32 decimals of land of plot 1250 and without noticing, such evidence on record decreed the suit covering entire 52 and 1/2 decimals on surmises and, as such, the judgment of the Trial Court is not a judgment at all and that the Appellate Court without adverting to those materials on record affirmed the judgment of the Trial Court without having regard to the Order 41, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and thereby, both the Courts committed error of law in decreeing the suit which is an error in the decision occasioning failure or justice. The learned Advocate submitted Kartik Chandra Biswas admittedly the auction purchaser allegedly granted patta in favour of plaintiff arid the proforma defendant No.11 Earuddin by alleged registered patta dated. 3-3-1956 but in fact, Kartik Chandra Biswas had no superior interest over the suit land at the relevant time, on tlie operation of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act stated on 13-12- 1955 at the locality and, as such, the.alleged patta is a void document. He further submitted tlre plaintiff has filed the suit only for declaration of title and confirmation possession without partition, as according to the plaintiff got the patta along with the proforma defendant No. 11 and, as such, the suit itself is not maintainable but this vital aspect of the case lost sight of the Courts below and decreeing the suit committed error of law which is an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He submitted further that the plaintiff only produced patta which has been marked as Exhibit 1 and no paper showing act of possession has been produced before the Court but the plaintiff has filed the suit and examined himself as PW 1 and 2 other witness PW 2 and 3 to support his possession, but those 2 witnesses only corroborated to the extent of 16 decimals of land and even such, materials on record the Courts below finding the title and possession of the plain- tiff oven the entire suit land had decreed the suit and thus committed error of law which is an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 11. The learned Advocate further submitted that the father of the defendant No.6 he had not purchased the land from Kartik Chandra Biswas and he had no onus to prove the title of Kartik, but Kartik Chandra Biswas sold his land to one Ataur Rahman by registered kabala dated 28-5-1969 and the father of the defendant No.6 being co-sharer filed the pre-emption case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the preemption was confirmed up to Appellate Court, but said Ataur Rahman did not move the higher Court against the judgment, passed by the Appellate Court. The father of the defendant No. 6 got possession pursuant to the order of the Court passed in preemption case and in spite of such materials on record the Trial Court Shifted the onus to the defendant No.6 to prove the case as to title of Kartik which was not at all necessary because the father of the defendant No.6 only being preemptor got the land by pre-emption sold to Ataur Rahman by Kartik and in this score also the Trial Court as well as the Appellate Court have committed error of law in not noticing such evidence on record and decreeing the suit committed error of law resulting, in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate submitted further that the father of the defendant No.6 after receiving the judgment, and order of preemption case got mutated his name in SA Khatian No. 1144 and paid the rents and all the documents were made exhibits being exhibit No. Ka, Kha, Ga series Gha, Uma, Cha etc but those exhibits were not at all considered by the Trial Court as well as Appellate Court but decreed the suit which is liable to be set aside as committed error of law which has occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate has also submitted that the name of Kartik Chandra Biswas was recorded in SA Khatian which has been marked exhibit Uma(1) to show that Kartik had title and possession over the suit land who transferred his interest to Ataur Rahman and defendant father being co-sharer filed the pre-emption case and got the pre-emption but this aspect of the case was not taken into consideration by the Courts below and having passed the impugned judgment committed error of law which is an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 "On the other hand, section 75 A, which was incorporated in 1954, came into operation only when a notification giving notice of the intention to undertake the preparation of the record of rights under section 17 (3) or of the compensation assessment roll under section 31 (1) had been given and it placed a complete embargo only on the subletting of any land in the khas possession of any rent-receiver within the area or areas specified in the notification and subletting, if made in contravention of the said section, was made null and void. The land so sublet was also to stand forfeited to the Provincial Government after the amendments made to the said section in 1956. The intention of this section appears to be that since after the acquisition of the interests of rent-receivers, rent-receivers were themselves to retain certain classes of retainable Khas lands as tenants directly under the Government, they should not be allowed to create further sub-tenancies under them. This was in keeping with the scheme of the acquisition Act, which was that after the acquisition of all rent-receiving interest anyone who held land within the province of East Pakistan should hold it as a tenant or raiyat directly under the government and not under anyone else as an intermediary. 

 15. The learned Advocate. finally submitted that in framing of suit the plaintiff has not sought reiief against the SA Khatian No. 1143 appearing in the name of the Kartik Chandra Biswas, and so also against the order of preemption affirmed up to Appellate Court and, as such, mere declaration of title on the face of such documents are not at all maintainable but the Courts below on the face of such record have failed to notice those infirmity in the framing of suit and having decreed the suit both the Courts committed fundamental error of law which is an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 17. The learned Advocate submitted that the patta dated 3-3-1956 is a document of more than 30 years old and has been produced by the plaintiff as contemplated under section 90 of the evidence Act and which has got presumption of genuineness of the document and having regard to such evidence on record the Courts below decreed the suit and committed to error of law in decreeing the suit. The learned Advocate has referred the case of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) vs Md Reasuddin Pk reported in 5 BLC (AD) 76. 

 18. The learned Advocate further submitted the suit for declaration of title in the present form is maintainable in as such as real owner having been in possession is not required to file suit merely because his land has been wrongly recorded in the records of right and he can filed suit for declaration of title when any claim is raised on the basis of wrong recording of rights and has relied upon a decision in the case of Government of the Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner. Feni vs Har Chandra Nath reported in 10 MLR (AD) 313. 

 "10. The learned Additional Attorney-General submitted that the plaintiffs were very such aware of the preparation of the wrong record of right from 28-12-1970 when they obtained the certified copy of the Khatian recording the land in suit in the name of the Government. It may be mentioned the law is now settled that a real owner is not required to file the suit merely because his land has been wrongly recorded in the record of rights and he can very much wait until the person in whose name the record of right has been wrongly prepared raised claim in the land of the rightful owner." 

 19. The learned Advocate has submitted further that the plaintiff has also title by adverse possession and the Trial Court also found that the possession of the plaintiff and recorded findings that the plaintiff acquired the title by adverse possession and referred to the decision in the case of Nurjahan Begum vs Nur Rahman reported in 59 DLR 98, wherein a Division Bench of this Court held: 

 20. The learned Advocate finally submitted that the plaintiff may be given an opportunity to seek appropriate remedy against the Khatian appearing in the name of Kartik and the orders passed in preemption case, remanding the suit to the Trial Court. The learned Advocate on the date of judgment has handed over Photostat copy DP Khatian 325/DP Khatian 859 and submitted that the name of the plaintiff has been recorded in the last khatian finding the plaintiff in possession and to that contention he refers to decision in the case of Erfan Ali vs Joynal Abedin Mia (late) represented by his legal heirs Golenur reported in 35 DLR (AD) 216. 

 "8. The rent-receipts were excluded from consideration by the lower Appellate Court taking the view that these are provisional receipts and that they carry little weight in that "any person interested in a land may pay rent to the Government Acquired Estate." This view is erroneous, for rent-receipts, though no documents of title are important items of evidence of possession any may be used as collateral evidence of title since possession generally follows title. Again plaintiff's name has also been recorded in the SA Khatian prepared in the period immediately following the whole-sale state acquisition in 1956 and all objections raised by defendant No. 1 were overruled by the Revenue-officer and then by the appellate authority. " 

 The Trial Court after considering the evidence PWs recorded findings that: 

 25. Upon analyses of the aforesaid evidence, pleading of the plaint along with the prayer and schedule and findings of the Trial Court, it appears that the Trial Court failed to notice that the plaintiff only submitted the patta deed 3-3-1956, exhibit-I and no papers showing his subsequent mode of possession has been produced before the Court. During the cross examination the PW 1 clearly stated that :“আমি নালিশী জমির খাজনা দেই না” and the name of the Kartik is still appearing in the khatians and such evidence clearly indicated that after the alleged patta the plaintiff did not take any step to record his land in the subsequent record of rights and admittedly, the plaintiff is not paying rent to the Government and no document had been produced .to show his possession in any manner in the suit land and the PW 2 and 3 only proved possession over 16 decimals of land out of 32 decimals of land in respect of plot No. 1250 but the plaintiff filed the suit for 52 and 1/2 decimals of land and thereby, it is clear that the plaintiff could not prove his title over the entire suit land as the PW 2 and 3 only allegedly corroborated to the extent of 16 decimals of plot No. 1250. 

 26. In view of the evidence on record, it is palpably clear that the plaintiff could not prove his possession over entire 52 II) decimals of land by any documentary or oral evidence and in this view of the matter, the findings of the Trial Court as well as Appellate Court appears based on total non consideration of the evidence on record and, as such, they committed serious error of law in not considering those aspect of the case and arriving at such conclusion and decreeing the suit. The defendant on the other hand submitted several documents which have been marked as exhibits from KaJha series. Exhibit 'ka' is the judgment and order passed in Misc. Case No. 523 of 1970 by which preemption was allowed, wherein the father of the defendant was the preemptor and on appeal the order of the Trial Court was affirmed (Annexure-Ka). It may be noted that Kartik sold his land vide exhibit-Cha(2) to Ataur Rahman by registered kabala deed dated 28-5-1969. The father of the preemptor being a co-sharer of the land instituted a preemption case No. 523 of 1970 in the Court of Munsif, 1st Court, at Magura and the pre-emption was allowed as aforesaid but no revision was preferred before the High Court Division and thereby, the judgment and order passed by the Trial Court as well as the Appellate Court remained, as such, and the defendant No.6 through his father having obtained possession pursuant to the order of the Court has been possessing the land and mutated his name, paid rents to the government and the defendants have filed those documents and marked as exhibits from Ga to Jha. On scrutiny of the judgment of the Trial Court, it has been found that the Trial Court has misconstrued the evidence and document as well as the orders of the competent Courts and upon such misinterpretation, misreading of evidence and records certain imaginary findings has been recorded and such findings, have been concurred by the Appellate Court. On perusal of the judgment of the Appellate Court, it appears that the Appellate Court mechanically affirmed the findings and decision of the Trial Court without adverting to the evidence to its proper perspective and upon, over all evaluation it further revels that the Courts below have committed gross illegalities in not considering the evidence to its proper perspective and thereby committed error of law resulting an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 27. Now let me deal with the legal aspect of the case. The defendant petitioner acquired the title through preemption case as a co-sharer of the case land which was sold by Kartik to Ataur Rahman. It appears in the pleadings of the parties that Kartik admittedly acquired the land from Shudhamay and got the possession through Court and annulled all the encumbrances by filing case No. 117 of 1953 under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Against the auction sale one Shudhanshu filed Suit No. 137 of 1956 for setting aside the aforesaid auction sale and the suit was dismissed and the sale was confirmed. Both the parties claim title through Kartik. The plaintiff allegedly took patta from Kartik on 3-3-1956 but thereafter, the plaintiff did not take any step to record his name in the relevant Khatian or mutated his name in the record and also admittedly has not paid rent to any authority, what so ever, since 1956. It is evident on record that the plaintiff has failed to show any papers showing possession except the patta and oral evidence of PW 1, 2 and 3. PWs 2 and 3 only allegedly proved possession over 16 decimals of land though the suit is for 52-1/2 decimals land. On the other hand the defendant claimed that after December 1955 the Kartik had no authority to grant patta holding rent receiving interest as rent receiving interest had already been ceased in view of publication of notification dated 13-12-1955 under sub-section 3 of section 17 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The defendant submitted that Kartik did not execute such patta as he had no superior interest. The plaintiff also did not take step to examine the signature of the Kartik in order to prove the patta. It has already been submitted that Kartik being owner recorded his name in the SA Khatians and being in possession sold land out of 3 plots vide exhibit-C to one Ataur Rahman and the father of the defendant No. 6 being co-sharer filed preemption case and got the preemption up to Appellate Court, but the plaintiff did never take any step to dislodge those SA Khatians as well as the sale deed executed by Kartik and so also the pre-emption case but remained silent. It appears further the defendant No. 11 who is the co-recipient of patta dated 3-3-1956 along with the plaintiff filed suit No. 115 of 1977 in the Court of Assistant Judge Magura and the defendant ultimately won the case in the Appellate stage contesting Title Appeal No. 485 of 1983 and on the face of such material evidence on record, the plaintiff did not take any step what so ever and such silence on the part of the plaintiff clearly proved that he failed to prove his patta deed and possession. It is on record that the defendant did not purchase land from Kartik but got the land of exhibit-'C' by preemption and, as such, from the evidence on record the defendant was not supposed to know about the basis of the acquisition of land by Kartik and, as such, defend in not bound to prove as to the acquisition of title by Kartik and in spite of such materials on record, Trial Court shifted the onus of proof upon the defendant and giving finding as such, it appears that the Courts below committed error of law. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite party has tried to establish title on the basis of patta but no cogent evidence has been adduced before the Court. The learned Advocate has relied upon several decisions as noted above to get the decree on the basis of the decisions inasmuch as on the basis of holding over, adverse possession and as well as findings of the Courts below as the Courts below, concurrently settled the facts in favour of the plaintiff but the decisions cited by the learned Advocate are not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case. 

 32. I have already found that the Courts below have not adverted to the evidence on record to its true perspective and interpreted the evidence and given findings only on surmises. The trend of recording of findings by the Trial Court, it appears that the Trial Court has recorded findings and drawn conclusion without being sure as to purport of the evidence and documents. The appears on perusal of the judgment of the Appellate Court that the Appellate Court on cursory view has affirmed the findings of the Trial Court which has not fulfilled the object of Order  rule 31 of Code of Civil Procedure and thereby, it appears that both the Courts committed error of law in not considering the oral and documentary evidence to its proper and decision having not been passed in accordance with law should be interfered. 

 Send down the lower Courts records immediately.

full_judgment:
2. Plaintiff Gangacharan Debnath and others filed Title Suit No. 10 of 1994 before the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Brahmanbaria (the trial Court) for declaration of their title to the property measuring an area of 15 decimals of homestead property of C.S Plot No. 1069, S.A Plot No. 1350 under Mouza, Police Station and District-Brahmanbaria (previously Tripura District) as described in the 2nu schedule of the plaint (hereinafter referred to as the suit property) and 23 decimals of pond of C.S Plot No. 1068, S.A Plot No. 1349 under Mouza, Police Station and District-Brahmanbaria (previously Tripura District) as described in the 3rd schedule of the plaint(hereinafter referred to as the suit pond) stating, inter alia, that the suit property and suit pond along with some other lands as described in the 1st schedule of the plaint originally belonged to Kunja Mohan Debnath (Kunja), Piyare Mohan Debnath (Piyare), Raj Mohan Nath (Raj) and Sarupa Sundari Nath (Sarupa). Their names were duly recorded in C.S khatian Nos. 632, 633 and 634 of C.S. Plot Nos. 1064, 1069, 1060, 1068 and 1063 for 83 decimals of land. Kunja died leaving behind wife Muktakeshi Nath (Muktakeshi) and daughter Suchitra Debi (Suchitra), Muktakeshi filed Title Suit No. 241 of 1933 against the father of the defendant Nos. 1-3 i,e. Banamali Debnath (Banamali), son of Piyare, Raj and others for partition of the 1st schedule property along with other properties. Mahananda Debnath (Mahananda), father of the plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 were added as defendant No. 4 in the said suit. The said suit being Title Suit No. 241 of 1933 was decreed on compromise. According to Solenama and final decree the plaintiff of partition suit Muktakeshi got 15 decimals of homestead land from C.S. Plot No. 1069, 05 decimals from C.S Plot No. 1064, 01 decimal from C.S. Plot No. 1062 and 10 /9 decimals i.e. 4/9 share from C.S. Plot No. 1068 out of 23 decimals. Banamali, father of the defendant Nos. 1-3 got 13 decimals of lands in some other plots and Chapala got 05 decimals. Muktakeshi by registered deed date 07.05.1942 sold the suit property and 5 ¾ decimals of the pond out of the suit pond in favour of Sanatan Debnath (Sanatan) and delivered possession to Sanatan. Suchitra got 05 decimals of land of C.S. Plot No. 1064 after the death of her mother. Banamali, father of the defendant Nos. 1-3 fraudulently created a deed of purchase from Suchitra, Thereafter, Banamali filed a pre-emption case against Sanatan in the 2nd Court of Munsif, Brahmanbaria in the year 1945. But that suit was dismissed on contest. Thereafter, Banamali filed another suit being Title Suit No. 20 of 1947 and the said suit was also dismissed on contest. Sanatan had been in exclusive possession of the suit property and 5 ¾ decimals share in the suit pond for more than 12(twelve) years. Thereafter, in 1952, he sold the suit property and his share to the suit pond in favour of Gangacharan Debnath (Gangacharan) plaintiff No. 1 and Mahananda, father of the plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 verbally on receipt of part consideration money. But Gangacharan and Mahananada could not pay the entire price for which the document of sale could not be registered. As they were relatives, Gangacharan and Mahananda did not deem it necessary for registration of a sale deed in their favour from Sanatan. The plaintiffs have been in possession of the suit property by erecting homestead thereon and enjoying their share of the suit pond with other co-sharers. Banamali once set fire to the house of the plaintiffs for which all the documents of the plaintiffs were burnt into ashes. The plaintiffs filed a criminal case and Banamali was convicted in the said case. Presently, the plaintiffs and defendant Nos. 1-3 and others have been in possession of the suit pond jointly as owners thereof. The defendants with false statements filed Miscellaneous Case No. 19 of 1993-1994 against mutation of the suit property in the names of the plaintiffs. Upon hearing, mutation of the suit property in the names of the plaintiffs was cancelled. However, the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Brahmanbaria observed that the 2nd schedule i.e. the suit property and the suit pond are in possession of the plaintiffs. The defendant Nos. 13 were never owners or possessors of the 2nd schedule property i.e. the suit property. Recently, after cancellation of the names of the plaintiffs in the mutation case, the defendants are claiming that they are the owners of the suit property. In the above backdrop, the plaintiffs filed the suit for declaration of their title to the above properties by adverse possession. 

 3. Defendant Nos. 1-3 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the averments made in the plaint of the suit contending, inter alia, that the suit property was duly recorded in the names of C.S. recorded owners and thereafter by amicable partition among the C.S. recorded owners Kunja and Sarupa got 58 decimals of land out of C.S. Plot Nos. 1069, 1068, 1064, 1060, 1063 and 1052 in their shares along with a share in the suit pond. 

 4. C.S. recorded tenant Mohan Nath while owner of C.S. Plot Nos. 1068 and 1064 measuring an area of 14 ½ decimals of land, died leaving behind 2(two) sons, namely, Puma Chand Debnath (Puma) and Banamali. The said sons became 8 annas owner each of the said property. While Kunja and Sarupa were in ejmali possession of 58 decimals of property, Sarupa died leaving behind Kunja as her sole heir. Kunja while owner of 29 decimals of land out of 58 decimals of land, gifted 29 decimals of land out of the said land to his wife Muktakeshi and grandsons Puma and Radhika. Radhika gifted his share to his wife Chapala. Chapala transferred the said land to Kali Mohan. Kunja while owner of the rest 29 decimals of land out of 58 decimals of land, died leaving behind wife Muktakeshi and daughter Suchitra as his heirs. Muktakeshi while owner of 29 decimals of land with Suchitra by inheritence and 9 2/3 decimals of land by way of gift from her husband, died leaving behind Suchitra as her sole heir. Suchitra became the owner of 38 2/3  decimals of land out of the said property and she due to legal necessity sold the said land to Banamali by a registered deed dated 24.02.1944 and delivered possession to him. Subsequently, the said deed was corrected as a plot number was wrongly recorded in the previous deed. But the said corrected deed was subsequently lost. Piyare while owner of 14 V2 decimals of land died leaving behind his son Puma and Banamali. They became the owners of the said land and also became the owner of 9 2/3 decimals of land from Kunja. Puma died unmarried leaving Banmali as his sole heir and Banamali became owner of total 62 2/3 decimals of land by way of inheritance and purchase and he had been in uninterrupted possession of the said land including the suit property and suit pond peacefully by exercising his own right for more than 12(twelve) years and his name was correctly recorded in the S.A. khatian. Mahananda, father of the plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 and their mother Indumoyee became shelterless after death of their father and they being relatives of Banamali, he permitted them to live in 08 decimals of land on the suit property and he was in possession of the rest 07 decimals of land out of it. Defendant Nos. 1-3 are now in possession of rest 07 decimals of land and also owner of 08 decimals of land. The plaintiffs were ejectable licensee of the defendants since the lifetime of their father but they collusively mutated their names relating to the suit property. Therefore, the defendants filed the miscellaneous case and the names of the plaintiffs were cancelled from the record-of-rights. Muktakeshi never filed any suit for partition against Banamali and Mahananda was not defendant No. 4 in the suit. Muktakeshi did not get 15 decimals of land of C.S. Plot No.1069 (suit property) and 109 decimals of land of C.S. Plot No. 1068 (suit pond). Muktakeshi neither sold the suit property to Sanatan by any registered deed nor he was in possession of the suit property at any time. The statements made in the plaint are all false and defendant Nos.1-3 are in possession of the suit property. The suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 6. The trial Court, upon hearing the parties and in consideration of evidence on record by judgment and decree dated 30.10.1997, decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs and declared the plaintiffs' title to 15 decimals of land in 3/4. S. Plot No. 1069 (suit property) and 5 ¾ decimals share in the suit pond. 

 11. Mr. Kamal-ul-Alam, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the appellants, has taken us through the various judgments and decrees passed by the trial Court, the Appellate Court, the High Court Division, the connected materials on record and put forward the following arguments before us: 

 3. Both the trial Court and the High Court Division though mainly decided the suit and revision considering Pourashava tax receipts issued from office of Brahmanbaria Pourashava (exhibit-6 series) and the rent receipt (exhibit-7), but both the Courts failed to notice that plot numbers were not mentioned in the said Pourashava tax receipts and those are only for the years 1991 to 1995 and the rent receipt is only for the year 1399 B.S. and the mutation in the names of the plaintiffs in the record-of-rights has been cancelled. The trial Court and the High Court Division without considering the value of those documents and the evidence on record erroneously decided that the plaintiffs proved their title to the suit property and the suit pond by way of adverse possession. 

 4. The decision of the Appellate Court relating to ownership and possession of defendant Nos. 1-3 relating to 07 decimals of land was correct as plaintiff No. 1 himself admitted it in his cross-examination. But the trial Court and the High Court Division without properly considering the evidence on record unlawfully decided that the plaintiffs are the owners of the entire suit property (2na schedule). 

 13. In reply, Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Senior Advocate appearing with Mr. Subrata Saha, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondents, takes us through the judgment and decree of various Courts and the evidence on record and contends as under: 

 c) The report relating to cancellation of plaintiffs' mutation also shows that the plaintiffs were/are in possession of the suit property. However, mutation in their names was cancelled as notices were not duly served upon all the co-sharers at the time of mutation of their names in the record-of-rights. 

 Examination of Records 

 16. We have examined the judgments and decrees of various Courts and the evidence on record. 

 17. It is an admitted proposition that C.S. recorded owners of the suit property and the suit pond along with other properties were Kunja, Raj, Piyare and Sarupa. The plaintiffs claimed their title to the suit property by adverse possession for the last 30/35 years. 

 20. The Appellate Court, on the other hand, allowed the appeal in part and declared the plaintiffs' title to 08 decimals of land (part of suit property) of C.S. Plot No. 1069 only by way of adverse possession in consideration of the evidence on record. 

 32. It appears from the evidence on record as discussed that the plaintiffs though could not produce the document of purchase of the suit property from Mulctakeshi by Sanatan or purchase of the suit property by Gangacharan and Mahananda from Sanatan, but they could prove their exclusive uninterrupted possession in the suit property by erecting four houses and living there for more than 30/35 years. On the other hand, the defendants' witnesses could not prove their possession. Rather, one of the defendants, D.W.1 admits that the suit property is a compact property with boundaries in four side of the land. 

 33. In consideration of the evidence on record, we are of the view that both the trial Court as well as the High Court Division properly decided that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit property uninterruptedly for more than 30-35 years. 

 We find no misreading or non-consideration of the evidence on record by the trial Court or the High Court Division. Therefore, the declaration of the plaintiffs' title to the suit property (C.S. Plot No. 1069, 2nd schedule property) appears to be lawful. It appears that the Appellate Court considering only a part of the statement made by P. W.1 during the cross-examination decided that the plaintiffs admitted possession of the defendants relating to 07 decimals of land without considering the whole statement of the P. W.1 erroneously.

lawyer:
Md Sajjad Ali Chowdhury with Abul Kashem Sarker Advocates -------- For the Petitioners, 
Md Khalilur Rahman, Advocate -------- For the Opposite Parties,
parties:
Abdul Latif (Md) -------- Petitioners
Vs.
 Mohammad Ali  -------- Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
8. Mr Md Sajjad Ali Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners, submits that the Court of appeal below passed the judgment and the decree without applying its judicial mind. He then submits that the judgment of the Court of Appeal below was passed in a slipshod manner and the Court did not discuss the evidence adduced by the parties. He further submits that the Courts below passed the judgments on mistaken views of law and facts and thus resulted in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He next submits that the Courts below have failed to frame any issue on the title and possession of the plaintiffs in the present Partition Suit although possession in a suit for Partition is very much material, which ought to have been decided by framing and discussing issues. He also submits that all the persons having interest of title in the suit property were not brought on record for the proper adjudication of the matter and as the defect of parties is a very vital question in a Partition Suit, non- impleading of interested persons is a sufficient ground for dismissal of the suit. 

 9. Mr Md Khalilur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties, files a counter-affidavit and submits that the plaintiffs have succeeded to prove their case and have obtained relief from the Courts below. He next submits that considering the facts, circumstances and the evidence on record, the trial Court granted saham in the Partition Suit to the plaintiffs and the Lower Appellate Court affirmed the judgment passed by the trial Court on the basis of materials on record and there being no error in the decision and more so, no failure of justice being occasioned to the defendant-petitioners, the Rule is liable to be discharged. The learned Advocate submits that the trial Court decreed the suit rightly and the Court of Appeal below very cogently and legally dismissed the appeal. He submits that the scope of interference with the concurrent findings of fact of the Courts below under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is very limited and when the concurrent findings of fact arrived at by the Courts below are supported by evidence on record and there being no error of law involving the case, there is no scope for interference in revision. In support to his contention, the learned Advocate has referred a decision as reported in 11 MLR 92. He points out that a mere denial by the defendant as to the title of the plaintiff in any portion of the property in a Partition Suit would not convert a Partition Suit into a declaratory suit for title and for possession and hence the contention that the Partition Suit is not maintainable without a declaratory suit for title, as it involves disputed question of title, as presented by the learned Advocate for the petitioner has no substance. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate has referred to a decision as reported in 34 DLR 127. 

 10. I have heard the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners and opposite parties and perused the revisional application, counter-affidavit along with other materials on record. It appears that the opposite party Nos. 1-3 as plaintiff filed a Suit for partition in respect of 6.91-123/145 decimals of land as stated in the schedule of the plaint. The trial Court decreed the suit in preliminary form in respect of 6.91 decimals of land and the Court of Appeal below on hearing the parties dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. In a Partition Suit, disputed questions of title may be involved and such questions are to be decided by the Court trying the suit. A mere denial by a defendant as to the title of the plaintiff in any portion of the property in a Partition Suit would not convert a Partition Suit into a declaratory suit for title and a suit for possession, as the jurisdiction of a Civil Court in case of a Partition Suit could not be placed at the mercy of every profligate defendant to render the Court a mere ministerial agent only to carry into effect the wishes of the parties in case where there were no matters of controversy between them. It cannot be said that the present Partition Suit is not maintainable without a declaratory suit for title as it involved disputed question of title. The plaintiff is entitled to maintain a Suit for Partition if his possession in some part of the joint property is admitted or established. Partition signifies the transformation of joint possession into separate possession and the suit does not cease to be one for partition, merely because the defendants denies the title of the plaintiff to a share of the estate or to specific land of the estate and asserts a hostile title and adverse possession therein as in the present case. It is the claim of the plaintiff that Sajimuddin, being not a very intelligent person, deputed Elimuddin for recording the record of rights of the disputed jote and as the settlement officers made their camp in the house of Elimuddin during the survey, taking advantage to that situation, Elimuddin got the record of rights recorded in his name along with others. The Courts below found that there was no reason for getting the property recorded in the name of Elimuddin and others and believed that Elimuddin got the property recorded in his name along with others in a collusive manner. The plaintiff claimed that on 5-2-1980, defendants Nos. 5 and 6 and plaintiff No. 1 entered into an agreement of compromise and agreed that the record in the name of Elimuddin was wrong in which defendants Nos. 5 and 6 put their signatures and the said compromise agreement was produced before the Court by the plaintiff by way of Exhibit 3 and the trial Court compared the signature of defendant No.6 as in the compromise agreement and in the written statement and determined that the signature is of the same person Md Abdul Latif. On consideration of the evidence, both oral and documentary, the trial Court came to the finding that the plaintiff is the co-sharer of the disputed jote and is entitled to get the saham of 6.91-123/145 decimals of land by virtue of inheritance and pattan. The Court of Appeal below affirmed the judgment of the trial Court. The appellate Court whether reversing or affirming the decision of the trial Court must independently consider the evidence on record but in the case of affirming the findings of the trial Court, the narration of the entire evidence and reiteration of the reasons given by the trial Court are not essential. In such a case, expressions of general agreement with those of the trial Court are generally considered sufficient. It is not the duty of the appellate Court when it agrees with the view of the trial Court on the evidence either to restate the effect of the evidence or to reiterate the reasons given by the trial Court. Expression of general agreement with reasons given by the Court decision of which is under appeal would ordinarily suffice. 

 11. It appears that the trial Court as well as the Lower Appellate Court considered all aspects thoroughly and concurrently found that the plaintiffs succeeded to prove their case. The decisions of both the Courts below, being based on facts, circumstances and evidence on record and there being concurrent findings over the points in issue and there being found no error of law or fact in passing the impugned judgment, I am of the opinion that the impugned judgment and decree do not warrant any interference by this Court. 

 12. Since both the Courts below on proper assessment of the evidence on record came to a concurrent finding, this finding is binding upon this Court unless it is shown that there is misreading or non-consideration of material evidence on record in arriving at such finding. The learned Advocate for the petitioners has failed to make out such a case. 

 13. The judgment of the Courts below are not tainted with legal infirmity and perversity justifying interference. After examining the record of the case and hearing the learned Advocates of both the parties, I am of the view that there are sufficient evidence and materials on record to come to the decisions which have been arrived at by the Courts below. 

 Send down the lower Court records and a copy of the judgment and order to the Court concerned.

lawyer:
M.A. Azim Khair, Deputy Attorney General, instructed by B. Hossain, Advocate-on-Record.   ------ For the Appellant 
Md. Mozaffar Hossain, Senior Advocate instructed by Md. Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record ------- For Respondent No.1 
Respondent No. 2 ------- Not represented.

Government of Bangladesh ------ Appellant
VS

full_judgment:
3. The case of the writ Petitioner, in short, is that the disputed premises namely F/G/7, Sher Shah Colony (Housing Estate) Chittagong was allotted to one Nazir Mohammad by registered deed of lease dated 04.06.1960. Nazir Mohammad while in possession sold the same to one Md. Safi by a registered kabala dated 17.04.1964. Md. Safi got his name mutated in the record of rights. Thereafter, Md. Safi entered into a conteract to sell the building and delivered possession to the writ petitioner and also executed a registered kabala dated 26.12.1980 in favour of the writ petitioner who after purchase applied for mutation of her name but the Assistant commissioner, Housing and settlement by memo dated 30.11.1982 informed her that mutation could not be allowed as the building had already been included in the list of abandoned buildings. Thereafter, she filed an application for release of the building and the Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong by his Memo dated 06.06.1985 recommended for release of the same to the Commissioner of Chittagong Division from the list of abandoned buildings. The further case is that Md. Shafi and she arc Bangladeshi nationals by birth and hence no permission for transfer of the property is required but still the building was not released and she was constrained to file the case before the Court of Settlement which after hearing arbitrarily dismissed the case. The petitioner then moved the High Court Division in writ jurisdiction and the High Court Division after hearing made the Rule absolute as noticed earlier. 

 5. Leave was granted to consider the submission that the High Court Division erred in law in setting aside the finding of facts arrived at on evidence on record by the Court of Settlement in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution like a court of appeal and the further submission that in view of the specific findings of the Court of Settlement that Md. Safi had not acquired any title to the building in question and for that matter the writ petitioner did not acquire any right, title and interest the High Court Division erred in law in entertaining the writ petition and setting aside the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement which rightly found that property was an abandoned one and the further submission that the High Court Division erred in law in finding that the Court of Settlement failed to decide the character of the property as to whether it is an abandoned property or not. 

 7. It is not disputed that the premises namely F/G/7, Sher Shah Colony (Housing Estate) Chittagong was allotted to one Nazir Mohammad by registered deed of lease dated 04.06.1960. Nazir Mohammad while in possession sold the same to one Md. Shafi by a registered kabala dated 17.04.1964. It is also undisputed that Md. Shafi got his name mutated in the record of rights. The Respondents' case is that Md. Shafi entered into a contract to sell the premises to the Writ Petitioner and delivered possession and also executed a registered kabala dated 26.12.1980 in favour of the writ petitioner. There is no evidence on record to show that Md. Safi was a non-local rather it is on record that he sometimes resided in Dhaka and some times in Chittagong and notices was served upon Md. Shafi in his address in Bangladesh as found by the Court of Settlement and his possession in the suit property was also found by the Court of Settlement. It is to be remembered Md. Shafi purchased the disputed premises in the year 1964 that is long before the coursing into force of P.O. 16 of 1972. 

 9. Therefore the contention of the writ petitioner that since Md. Shafi is a national of Bangladesh by birth no permission of transfer of property in her favour was required appears to have substance. Since it has been proved that Md. Shafi purchased the property in 1964 by a registered kabala and he is a citizen of Bangladesh by birth and notices upon him were served by the Government in his address in Bangladesh and he got his name mutated in the record of right and paid rent/taxes to the Government, by no means of imagination it can be said that the disputed property is abandoned property. Therefore, the transfer by Md. Shafi to the writ petitioner did not require any permission and the same is a valid transfer. Hence, the disputed property did not assume the character of abandoned property. 

 10. In our view, that the High Court Division upon correct assessment of the materials on record, rightly decided that the suit property is not abandoned property.

lawyer:
A. J. Mohammad Ali, Senior Advocate instructed by A. K. M. Shahidul  Huq, Advocate-on-Record. ------ For the Petitioners

full_judgment:
2. The predecessors of the present petitioners, as plaintiffs, instituted Other Suit No.150 of 1986 before the Court of Assistant Judge, Satkania against the present respondents for declaration of title, confirmation of possession and also for perpetual injunction in respect of 1.3875 acres of land out of 1.85 acres in 12 annas share which was fully described in the; schedule to the plaint. The case of the plaintiffs, in short, is that the property in schedule to the plaint is a tank and the bank surrounding it which is popularly known as "Butter Pukur". That in the Moghi Chitta Survey the schedule property was recorded as Taraf Syed Mohammad Arshad Kishmat Malik Rahman. That the owner of the Taraf being a resident of distant place never possessed the same and the same was under adverse possession of Abdul Aziz son of Hamid Baksha and Abdul Fattah son of Munshi Ali Baksha for more than the statutory period of limitation. That during C.S. operation the Government enlisted the suit land as Nayabad Mohal and as per possession of Abdul Aziz and Abdul Fattah recorded their names under Jote No.5. That Abdul Aziz and Abdul Fattah possessed the tank for more than 90 years by payment of rents to the Government. That the said tank became silted up and Abdul Aziz and others settled the same to Mofzulur Rahman, Abdul Gafur, Abdul Bari and Ali Hossain the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 32-62. That Mofzulur and others having been in possession of the said tank re-excavated the same at huge cost and on behalf of the settlement holders their elder brother Ali Hossain received the receipt from the labourers for re-excavation of the tank. That Ali Hossain was literate person and acted as "Karjakark" on behalf of all family members. That in R.S. record of rights the tank was recorded in the names of Abdul Rajjak and others sons of Abdul Aziz and Faruk Ahmed and others-sons of Abdul Fattah with a note of permissive possession of Ali Hossain and others. That the surveyors and employees inadvertently recorded such wrong note of permissive possession of Ali Hossain and others instead of recording their names as tenants in corfa right. That after promulgation of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1951 the predecessors of the plaintiffs became the raiyats under the Government and the plaintiffs have been possessing the said tank on payment of rents. That upon an application made by the predecessor of the defendant No. 32 under Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a proceeding under Section 145 of the said Code being Miscellaneous Case No. 8 of 1949 was started in respect of the suit property and in that case the learned Magistrate found right and title of Golam Sultan and others sons of Ali Hossain and put them in possession of the suit property. That thereafter the predecessor of the plaintiffs had been possessing the suit tank by rearing and preserving fish therein and by planting trees on the bank of the tank within the knowledge of the defendants. That the plaintiffs had no good relation with the proforma defendant Nos. 32-62 the descendants of Ali Hossain and as such they have been made proforma defendants in the suit. That the principal defendants have no right, title, interest and possession in the suit tank, but they gave out in the locality that the suit tank was taluki property of Azmatullah and Muzibullah and  that the same was purchased by Ezzad Ali and others in auction and subsequently the predecessor of the defendants took settlement of the suit tank from them. That the principal defendants, who are rich men, have been making plan to forcibly enter into the suit tank, take away the trees therefrom and construct house thereon and thus the plaintiffs have been constrained to file the suit for declaration of title, confirmation of possession and for permanent injunction in respect of 12 annas shares in the schedule property. 

 3. The predecessors of the present respondent Nos. 1-19 as defendant Nos. 1-4 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement. These defendants denied the material case of the plaintiffs and stated, inter-alia, that the suit is not maintainable as it is barred by principle of res-judicata. The positive case of the defendant Nos.1- 4, in short, is that the suit property which is known as "Burrer Pukur" was recorded in Moghi Chita Survey as Plot No.699 under Taraf Syed Md. Arshad. That Azmatullah and Mujibullah became the tenants under Taraf through settlement. That for arrear rent the suit property was put into auction and Ijjat Ali, Mosharrof Ali and Anwar Ali purchased the same in auction and got possession thereof. That the said auction purchasers subsequently settled this property to Ali Mahmud on 25th falgun, 1257 B.S. Ali Mahmud possessed the suit tank by rearing and preserving fish and the bank by planting and collecting usufructs thereof. Thereafter Ali Mahmud died leaving behind two sons namely Abdul Ali and Nazir Ali. On 22.07.1280 B.S. Nazir Ali transferred his share in favour of Abdul Ali by registered kabala and in the said kabala Ali Hossain the predecessors of the plaintiffs was an attesting witness. That Abdul Ali became sole owner of the suit tank and constructed house on the bank of the tank. That the landlord collected rent from Abdul Ali and others through Rent Suit Nos.765 of 1914 and 1397 of 1918. That meanwhile the suit tank was recorded in plot Nos.611 and 612 in the names of Abdul Aziz and Abdul Fattah in the cadastral survey. That such record was wrong and baseless. That the Government acquired no right or title in the suit land and it was never taken as khas land of the Government. That the tank was never included in Nayabad Mahal. That Abdul Aziz and Abdul Fattah never possessed the suit tank. That preparation of the R.S. record of rights following the C.S. record of right in the names of Abdul Aziz and others was equally wrong and never acted upon. That the predecessors of the plaintiffs and proforma defendant Nos. 32 62 created and fabricated the so called unregistered patta dated 10.05.1913. "That the said so called patta is seen to be written after 21/22 years of purchase of the stamps. That the predecessor of the plaintiffs claimed the suit land as their purchased land in Other Suit No.17 of 1957, but failed to produce any kabala and never pointed out the existence of patio dated 10.05.1913. That at the time of R.S. operation the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 1-4 Abdul Ali went to Rengun for earning money and he entrusted his brother-in-law Ali .Hossain-the predecessors of the plaintiffs to get the tank recorded in his name, but Ali Hossain got the tank fraudulently recorded in the names of Syed Abdul Aziz and others with a note of permissive possession of Ali Hossain. That after returning from Rengoon Abdul Ali died leaving behind defendant No.1 and Jobbar Ali as two sons and two daughters. That the defendant No.1 and his brother Jobbar Ali and sister Amena Khaton instituted Other Suit No. 17 of 1957 and obtained a decree declaring their title in the suit tank. That thereafter defendant Nos. 1-14 and 15 of the said suit filed two different appeals being Nos. 498 of 1958 and 27 of 1959 before the District Ridge which were dismissed on contest and thereafter Second appeal being No. 505 of 1963 was filed before the High Court Division which also was dismissed. That the plaintiffs never had any title or possession in the suit tank and as such the suit filed by them is liable to be dismissed. 

 "Because by way of patta C.S. and R.S. record was duly prepared in the names of the predecessors of the present   petitioners and have been in continuous possession since 90 years;  that on the basis of patta the plaintiff produced "Dakhila" in the trial court which was exhibited without objection that the defendants could not prove that the dakhila was illegal, forged or otherwise created; that the lower appellate court also affirmed the findings of the trial court, but the learned High Court Division without considering the same and out of misreading and misinterpretation of the evidences illegally made the Rule absolute holding that the patta was not genuine and as such the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be interfered with by this Hon'ble Court."

full_judgment:
6. The case of the defendant No. 6 in short, is that the suit land belonged to Nabu Sheik @ Amir Sheik. Said Nabu Sheik @ Amir Shiekh while was owning and possessing the suit land died leaving behind three sons Naimuddin, Kedu and Elim. That the defendant Nos. 1-8 are the heirs and successive heirs of three sons of Nabu Sheikh @ Amir Sheikh. That these defendants have been possessing the suit land within full knowledge of the plaintiffs and their predecessors since long. That the S.A record of rights of the suit land is wrong, the plaintiffs have managed the S.A. record prepared in their names. The R.S. record also has been prepared wrongly on the basis of this wrong S.A. record. That the plaintiffs did not acquire any right, title and possession in the suit land by virtue of the wrong records of right. 

 8. Mr. Golam Arshad, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners has made submission to the effect that the High Court Division without examining the evidence on record and without considering the facts and circumstances discharged the Rule erroneously; that there are ample evidence on record and also facts and circumstances to prove the plaintiffs prima facie title and exclusive possession in the suit land and on consideration of these facts and circumstances the trial court decreed the suit rightly, but the Court of appeal below and the High Court Division without examining these evidence on record and facts and circumstances most whimsically dismissed the suit of the plaintiffs. The learned Advocate has argued that the plaintiffs have adduced sufficient oral evidence to prove their exclusive possession in the suit land and both the record of rights have been prepared in the names of the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs have paid rent to the Government regularly and produced rent receipt before the trial Court which were marked as exhibits and that all of those are sufficient to prove the plaintiffs' possession in the suit land. The learned Advocate has pointed out also that besides these evidence there are other important facts and circumstances which also strongly support the plaintiffs' possession in the suit land. The learned Advocate has pointed out that in this case, admittedly, the defendant Nos. 1-5 and 7-8 filed Solenama with the plaintiffs admitting the plaintiffs' title and possession in the suit land and has submitted that this fact is a very strong circumstance to support of the plaintiffs' claim in the suit land, but the appellate Court below and the High Court Division without considering all these facts and circumstances arrived at a finding that the plaintiffs court not prove their possession in the suit land, which is most erroneous. 

 9. Mr. Syed Mahbubur Rahman, the learned Advocate-on-record appearing for the respondent has made submission supporting the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. 

 10. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides and gone through the impugned judgment of the High Court Division and those of the appellate Court below and the trial Court and other materials on record. 

 "I. Because the High Court Division overlooked the very important aspect of the case that out of 8 defendants only one defendant the defendant No. 6 has denied the compromise petition which is a weighty piece of evidence in favour of plaintiffs' title and possession in the suit land; that the records of right along with rent receipts showing payment of rent for  a long period also gave a presumption of possession in favour of the plaintiffs, but the High Court Division did not consider these valuable evidence also and consequently came to the wrong findings and decision and as such the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is liable to be set aside."

lawyer:
Mr. Md. Abdus Salam Mondal with Mr. Surojit Bhattachargee, Advocates ------ For the appellants
