lawyer:
Probir Neogi Senior Advocate, instructed by Mrs. Sufia Khatun Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Petitioners 
A.M. Amin Uddin Senior Advocate, instructed by Md. Ashraf-uz-Zaman Advocate-on-Record -----For Respondent Nos.1, 8, 10 & 14 
Respondent Nos. 2-7, 9, 11-13, 15-30 ------ Not represented
parties:
Ramesh Chandra Das and others ----- Petitioners
Vs
Gopal Chandra Majumder being dead his heirs: 1(Ka) Sureshwar Majumder and others ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
3. The case of the plaintiffs, in brief, is that the suit properties belonged to Satish Mohon Roy, who has two sons namely Sushil Mohon Roy and Narayan Chandra Roy, 4 daughters namely Purno Shashi, Charu Bala, Swadeshi Bala and Bina Bala. Purno Shashi was married with Shubol Chandra Das, son of Subodh Chandra Das. Except Purno Shashi Das, the sons and other daughters left for India, where they started residing as their permanent abode and in spite of earnest request by Satish Mohon Roy, they did not return to Bangladesh. Purno Shashi Das and her husband Subol Chandra Das came to the homestead of Satish Mohon Roy and started to reside there taking care of Satish Mohon Roy. Subsequently, Satish Mohon Roy executed a Will in favour of Purno Shashi Das on 03.01.1962 appointing Subol Chandra Das as executor of the Will. Purna Shashi Das and her husband Subol Chandra Das continued to reside with Satish Monon Roy by looking after him. Thereafter, Satish Mohon Roy died and, subsequently, Subol Chandra Das, executor of the Will initiated Probate Case No.19 of 1963 and the learned District Judge granted probate on 01.07.1963 in favour of Purno Shashi Das. Subsequently, Subol Chandra Das, transferred the suit land to Gopal Chandra Majumder, Dilip Majumder and Joydeb Majumder-plaintiff Nos.1-3, Jitendra Chandra Majumder, father of plaintiff Nos.4-6 and grandfather and father-in-law respectively of plaintiff Nos.7 and 8 vide five sale deeds and delivered possession thereof. The plaintiffs mutated their names in the record of rights, paid rent and continued to hold and possess the same by themselves and through tenants. The defendants were monthly ejectable tenants, but they were habitual defaulter in payment of rent and in spite of repeated demand they didn't pay rents. Subsequently, on being approached, the Martial Law authority issued notice to the defendants to quit the suit properties. 

 6. The trial Court, upon hearing the parties and considering the evidence and materials on record by its judgement and decree dated 04.11.2012 decreed the suit. Being aggrieved, the defendants filed First Appeal No.03 of 2013 before the High Court Division, which upon hearing the parties was dismissed. Hence, the defendants are now before us having filed the instant civil petition for leave to appeal. 

 7. Mr. Probir Neogi, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submitted that the High Court Division failed to consider that the plaintiffs failed to prove the existence of the probate case and while the trial Court during trial called for the records of the pro-bate case, the concerned office could not produce the records and it transpires that the Will as well as probate case is totally false and forged. He further submitted that the plaintiffs claimed that Satish Chandra Roy executed a Will in favour of his daughter Purna Shashi Dasya on 03.01.1962 by appointing Subol Chandra Das as executor and they got probate on 01.07.63, but at that time the legal heirs of Satish Chandra Roy were not made party in the probate proceeding, and as such the probate was illegal and no right accrued in favour of Purna Shashi against the right of inheritance of Narayan Chandra Roy, and as such the impugned judgement and decree is illegal and cannot be sustained in law. He also submitted that the High Court Division failed to notice that the daughter of the executor of the Will had no right to transfer any land to any body and daughter of Satish Mohan did not execute any deed in favour of the plaintiffs and even did not give any power for which the plaintiffs never acquired any right, title and interest in the suit land and as such the instant suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession is not maintainable, but the High Court Division erred in decreeing the suit and thus the same is liable to be set aside. 

 9. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgement and order of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record. 

 10. We note from the judgement of the trial Court that upon elaborate discussion of the facts and circumstances and the evidence on record it was found that the predecessor of the plaintiffs obtained title to the suit land through probate of the Will executed by the original owner of the land, namely Satish Mohon Roy. It was observed by the trial Court that the suit property was recorded in the name of Purna Shashi Dasya, daughter of Satish Mohon Roy, in the S.A. Khatian and neither the defendants nor the predecessor of the defendants namely Narayan Chandra Roy raised any question regarding the S.A. Khatian. It was further observed that neither Satish Mohon Roy nor any of his heirs challenged the Will executed by Satish Mohon Roy. It was also observed that the name of Puma Shashi Dasya was recorded in R.S. Khatian No. 2529 and on her behalf her husband Subol Chandra Das transferred the suit land by way of 5 separate deeds in the year 1981 in favour of the plaintiffs, who thereafter mutated their names in respect of the suit land. The trial Court concluded that Narayan Chandra Roy therefore had no title to transfer by way of the disputed deeds dated 1996 and 1998. Accordingly, the trial Court decided that the plaintiffs were able to prove their title in the suit property and decreed the 5 disputed deeds detailed in schedule that to the plaint as void. 

 12. The High Court Division observed that in challenging the eviction notices by way of Title Suit No. 93 of 1991 the defendant intended to assert that they tendered rent to the plaintiffs on behalf of Narayan Chandra Roy, son of Satish Chandra Roy, but that contention is not sustainable as they failed to submit any paper showing payment of rents to Narayan Chandra Roy. Subsequently, they sought to amend the plaint claiming purchase of the suit property from Narayan Chandra Roy by a registered instrument. The High Court Division concluded that the above conduct of the defendant shows that they shifted from their earlier position raising a claim of ownership and thereby forfeited rights as tenant in the suit property. 

 13. It is clear from the facts and circumstances discussed above that the defendants by their own admission made in Title Suit No. 91 of 1993 (originally Title Suit No. 98 of 1984) were tenants in the suit property. It is also apparent from the evidence and materials on record, as observed and decided by the trial Court, that Purna Shoshi Dasya's name was recorded in the record of rights in respect of the suit property and that she had title in the suit property by way of Probate Case No.19 of 1963. The trial Court found that Narayan Chandra Roy did not have any title to pass to the defendants and hence, the disputed deeds were void.
case_type_name: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal

lawyer:
Abdul Quayum, Senior Advocate with Md Ali Reza and Abdul Matin Khasru, Advocates ------ For the Petitioners.
AJ Mohammad Ali with JN Deb and Chanchal Kumar Biswas, Advocate ------ For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Motleb Khan and others ------ Petitioners 
Vs
Md Majid Mollah and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
The was Rule issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 25-8-2008 and 31-8-2008 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Patuakhali in Title Appeal No. 171 of 2006 disallowing the appeal affirming those dated 20-11-2006 and 27-11-2006 respectively passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Patuakhali in Title Suit No. 41 of 2000 should not be set-aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the present petitioners as plaintiffs instituted the original suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession being Title Suit No. 41 of 2000 in the 1st Court of learned Joint District Judge, Patuakhali, contending inter alia that the suit property appertaining to Mouza Kudbar Char under Mirjaganj police station corresponding to CS Khatian No. 145 measuring an area of 4.12 acres of land originally belonged to one Kasem Ali Kha and Kazem Ali Kha. The CS record was correctly prepared in their names. The original owners died issueless and the property devolved upon their cousin Arman Kha. In the CS Khatian No. 142 the land measuring 8.25 acres have been recorded in the name of Arman Kha. At the demise of Arman Kha his three sons namely Ismail Kha, Asmat Kha and Jonab. Ali Kha inherited the property. In the petty settlement Khatian Nos. 108, 140/2 measuring 3.29 acres of land was recorded in the names of three brothers. Ismail Kha died leaving two daughters Jarina and Urful Nessa and two full brothers Asmat and Jonab All Kha. Urful died leaving behind one son, two daughters who are the plaintiff Nos. 41, 42 and 43. The plaintiffs who are 44 in numbers are the heirs and successive heirs of the recorded owners who possess the suit land for more than 12 years without any break. During settlement operation 2.25 acres of land was recorded in the names of the plaintiffs and the rest has been recorded in the names of the defendants. The plaintiffs have got their paternal homestead in the suit property. The defendants have no manner of title, interest and possession over the suit land but on the basis of wrong SA record they denied the title of the plaintiffs which constrained the plaintiffs to institute the original suit. 

 3. The contrary case of the defendant in short is thus that the superior landlord of the plaintiffs' predecessors was MT Brown Estate under Court of Wards and the land of CS Khatian No. 145 was auction purchased by the superior landlord. Beside this the land of CS Khatian No. 142 was also sold in a certificate case and was purchased by the superior landlord. The Court of Wards took possession of the land through court against which the predecessor of the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 139 of 1945 challenging the auction sale which was dismissed for default. Subsequently, the Court of Wards granted settlement in favour of one Jonab Ali by granting 'dakhilas' and those properties have been recorded in the name of the defendants during Revisional Settlement and State Acquisition operation. The land of Petty Settlement Khatian No. 108 was purchased by the government and the government resettled the same in part to the defendants and in part to the plaintiffs. Apart from this, the land of PS Khatian No. 140/2 was auction purchased by government for arrear of rent and the government leased out the same to the predecessor of the defendant Jonab Ali and one Nawab Ali Mia. The further case of the defendants is such that the SA Khatian has been correctly prepared in their names and they had been owning and possessing the suit land after construction of homestead and they have donated 0.30 acres of land in favour of the government for establishment of a 'Hat'. 

 4. The learned trial court after taking evidence from the sides of the respective parties dismissed the suit on contest on 20-11-2006. Being aggrieved the plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal No. 171 of 2006 in the Court of learned District Judge, Patuakhali which was heard and disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge, Patuakhali and the learned lower appellate court by the impugned judgment and decree disallowed the appeal affirming the judgment and decree passed by the trial court. 

 7. The learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that both the courts below in passing the judgment and dismissal decree and in disallowing the appeal committed illegality and irregularity resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocates further submits that none of the courts considered the facts of the case as to the effect that no paper has been filed to substantiate the delivery of possession pursuant to alleged settlement in favour of defendant-opposite parties. There has been total non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning miscarriage of justice. There is no paper from the side of the defendants that MT Brown Estate ever managed the property under the management of court of Wards and there is no evidence to show that the alleged settlement was granted in favour of the defendant by the Court of Wards. Both the Courts below on surmise and conjecture holding the correctness of the alleged settlement and auction purchase committed error of law. Neither the trial court nor the appellate court considered that there is no evidence of annulment and taking possession of the land by the government. Petty Settlement Khatian marked Exhibits-'Ka-3' and 'Ka-4' shows that the government was not the land-lord which is also not considered by the courts below. It was the case of the plaintiffs that Jonab Ali the predecessor of the defendants created the papers of auction and settlement by the act of fraud and forgery which has vitiated the alleged auction and settlement. The learned Advocates also submit that the courts below misdirected themselves on the question of payment of rent which is on the basis of wrong SA Khatian which has no presumptive value of correctness. The courts below also not considered the evidence of the defendant's witness No.6 who has admitted the possession of the plaintiff-petitioners and their homestead. The learned Advocates lastly submit that it is the case of the defendants that they took pattan from the landlord through 'amaldari dakhila' not by kabuliat. The CS khatian is a title document which proves the bona fide of the plain-tiffs and the evidence adduced from the side of the parties not properly assessed by the learned lower appellate court in its true perspective and there is non-reading and misreading of evidence and non-consideration to material facts in disposing the appeal which is violative to the provisions laid down under Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree is not sustainable. 

 8. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned counsels of the petitioners the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the opposite parties opposing the Rule submits that the defendants admit the CS Khatian in the name of the plaintiffs predecessor-in-interest They also admit the title of Arman Kha. But the fact remains that MT Brown Estate the superior landlord for arrear of rent auction purchased the suit land. Subsequently, the defendants were granted settlement. The learned Advocates further submits that both the courts below concurrently held that the plaintiffs are not entitled to get the relief as prayed for since they have no right, title, interest and possession in the suit property. The learned Advocates also submit that the plaintiffs to the suit by subsequent amendment of their plaint challenged the settlement and auction purchase of the defendants in their pleadings. Therefore, the onus of proof totally lies upon the plaintiffs to disprove the auction purchase and settlement of the defendants. The plaintiffs during trial of the original suit failed to discharge their onus in proving their pleading. The learned Advocates lastly submits that the plaintiffs have admitted after amending their original plaint that the recent khatians i.e. record of rights has not been prepared in their names but has been prepared in the names of the defendants. Those khatians have been wrongly prepared, which is the case of the plaintiffs and as a result of that the onus of proof is on the plaintiffs to prove that the SA khatian is wrongly prepared in the names of the defendants. The plaintiffs to the suit also alleged that the certificate sale, auction purchase and subsequent settlement taken by the defendants from the auction purchasers are fraudulent, collusive and not acted upon. Therefore, obviously under sections 101 and 103 of the Evidence Act the onus of proof is on the plaintiffs to prove their respective plea i.e. their case which does not lie on the defendants. Even then, the defendants under the provisions of Evidence Act after calling the volume book and necessary papers showing the certificate sale and auction purchase proved their case and after adducing evidence to that effect have proved that the tenancy of the original owners have been extinguished by virtue of auction sale as cited from the side of the defendants. All the documentary evidence has been properly evaluated by both the courts below and all the evidence on records has been properly assessed in its true perspective before arrival at a decision as to the merit of the suit and its subsequent appeal. There is no misreading or non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice by which the impugned judgment and decree can be interfered with. 

 10. On perusal of the case record it transpires that during trial of the original suit both the parties adduced evidence in support of their respective pleadings. It is an admitted position that the CS khatian Nos. 142 and 45 corresponding to RS khatian Nos. 108 and 140/2 marked Exhibits-1, 1(Ka), 1(Kha) and l(Ga) stands recorded in the names of Kazem Ali Kha. It is also admitted from the sides of the respective parties that the plaintiffs are the heirs and successive heirs of the CS and PS recorded tenants. It is the specific contention of the contesting defendants that the land of CS khatian Nos. 142 and 145 was put into certificate proceedings being Nos. 149 and 150 of 1933-34 and in that certificate cases the property was put to an auction. The superior landlord MT Brown Estate auction purchased the same which was duly affected on 20-6-1934 AD. In support of this the defendant-opposite parties produced the bainanama of the certificate proceeding marked Exhibit-'Ga' and 'Gha'. Besides this, it is apparent from the face of the records that during pendency of the original suit under the purview of Evidence Act to prove the certified copy of the bainanama the defendants called for the volume books from Patuakhali Sub-registry office. The concerned record-keeper after bringing the volume books proved the same which go on to show that one Poresh Nath Sen, Manager, Court of Wards on behalf of MT Brown Estate auction purchased the land in dispute. It is also evident from the documents on record that the predecessor of the plaintiffs for cancellation of the auction sale instituted a Title Suit being No. 129 of 1945 in the 3rd Court of the then Munsif, Patuakhali. That suit was dismissed for default. For restoration of the suit the plaintiffs to that suit preferred a Miscellaneous Case being No. 264 of 1946 which was also dismissed on 25-7-1946. To substantiate the aforesaid facts the certified copy of the Suit Register was produced which are Exhibit-'Uma' and 'Cha' respectively. It is the concurrent findings and decision of the courts below that the title of the plaintiffs predecessors has been extinguished by virtue of certificate proceeding and auction sale and in this way the plaintiffs having no manner of right, title and interest in the disputed property are not in a position to get the relief sought for. 

 11. It is a fact that the SA record of rights has got no presumptive value of correctness but it would prevail until and unless it is rebutted. While both the parties adduced evidence in support of their pleadings the onus of proof under the ambit of Evidence Act lies on the parties to prove their respective cases as stated in their pleadings. Consulting the case records it is obvious, to note that the primary onus of proof which was upon the defendants was discharged in proving their bonafide but vis-a-vis despite the pleadings of the defendants have been specifically challenged and denied by the plaintiffs by subsequent amendment of their plaint but that onus of proof was not discharged by producing cogent, tangible evidence from the plaintiff's side. Having gone through the records I find that the witnesses produced from the sides of the parties have been properly assessed by the Courts below. The trial court in his observation and findings discussed the testimony of the witnesses and scrutinizing the evidence on records it is noticed that the plaintiff No.  26 Abdul Latif Khan as witness No. 1 tried to establish their case who deposed on behalf of all the plaintiffs. This witness admits in his deposition that the RS and SA khatians stands recorded in the name of the defendants and prior to this despite he denied that their predecessor-in-interest for setting aside the certificate cases instituted a Title Suit being No. 139 of 1944 which was dismissed on 20-6-1946 and against that the Miscellaneous Case No. 246 of 2006 was also dismissed but the fact remains that the documentary evidence which are produced makes it clear that the predecessor of the plaintiffs actually for cancellation of the certificate proceeding instituted the suit but failed. To substantiate the position of the plaintiffs they have adduced two witnesses and consulting their testimony it can be easily held that they have hopelessly failed to prove the plaintiffs title and possession as alleged over the disputed property. They even do not know the disputed property practically. On the contrary, the defendants in support of their case examined 5(five) witnesses. All the witnesses have been thoroughly discussed by the trial court in his observation and findings and I find nothing non-consideration, misreading or non-reading of evidence and non-appreciation of the actual position of law. It is the established principle of Civil Law that the plaintiffs shall have to stand on their own legs and they cannot bank upon their adversary. In the instant suit after consulting evidence I have the reason to incline such a view that the plaintiffs' to the suit have failed to discharge their onus in proving their respective pleadings. 

 12. Consulting the case records it appears that no such material contradiction, omission or perverse findings is noticed by dint of which it can be held that there has been any sort of illegality in deciding the fate of the suit and its subsequent appeal. In our revisional jurisdiction, scope of interference under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is very limited. Only where it is noticed that there has been misreading or non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material facts or the observation and findings is based upon gross misconception of law or otherwise perverse which is contrary to law, evidence and records; only in that case the judgment and decree of the appellate court can be interfered with. In the instant case as I have already discussed earlier, no such material is transpired by which I can draw such interference that the impugned judgment and decree deserve my interference. 

 13. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs, the impugned judgment and decree dated 25-8-2008 and 31-8-2008 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Patuakhali, in Title Appeal No. 171 of 2006 disallowing the appeal affirming those dated 20-11-2006 and 27-11-2006 respectively passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Patuakhali in Title Suit No. 41 of 2000 is hereby affirmed. 

 14. The order of status quo granted earlier by this Court at the time of issuance of the Rule stands vacated. 

 Communicate the judgment and order at once and send down the lower Court's records immediately.

Bangladesh and others ----- Petitioners
Vs
Sirajul Islam and another ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
3. The plaintiff's case put in a nutshell are that suit land was belonged to kali Prasanna Chakraborty and others and their names were recorded in CR Khatian No. 251. Junab Ali the predecessor of plaintiffs and Kala Mia took settlement of the suit land with other lands from them through dakhila (rent receipt) dated 10-10-1950 BS. Since then they are exercising their right, title and possession in suit land by payment of rents to landlord and Government successively. Subsequently their names were recorded in SA Khatian No. 303 and mutation Khatian No. 1265 was opened in their names. Afterwards one Nurul Islam claimed title of suit land, which was challenged by Junab Ali in Title Suit No. 77 of 1980 and was decreed on compromise on 21-4-1980. Thereafter, Government enlisted the suit land as vested and non-resident property which was also challenged in Title Suit No. 1 of 1982, which decreed on contest on 30-5-1083. The plaintiffs as heirs of Junab Ali exercising their right, title and possession in suit land but Government threatening them to dispossess. Hence the suit. 

 4. Defendants contested the suit by filing written statement denying all material allegations made in plaint contending inter alia that the suit land was acquired by the Government in LA Case No. 11 of 1921-22 for public purpose to establish Burichang charitable dispensary, since then they are in possession by constructing a house functioning as dispensary. The suit land was wrongly recorded in the names of predecessors of plaintiffs ultimately it was corrected, now it stands in the name of Government. The plaintiffs have no right, title and possession in suit land. Thus the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 9. In order to appreciate their submissions I have gone through the records and given my anxious consideration to their submissions. 

 11. On going to materials on record, it transpires that suit land was belonged to Kali Prasanna Chakraborty and others, plaintiffs claim that suit land was settled to their predecessor Junab Ali and Kala Miah through a rent receipt dated 10-10-1950 BS (Exhibits 2 and 6). Since then they are in possession. Defendants disowned such facts. They claim that the suit land was acquired in LA Case No. 11 of 1921-22 (Exhibits T-Y), Since then they are in possession by constructing a house functioning as Burichang Charitable Dispensary. 

 13. With regard to the submissions advanced as to sending back the suit on remand, I am of the view that evidences and all materials are there on record, so it is useless to send back suit on remand for causing unnecessary delay in disposal of suit. Therefore, I am inclined to dispose of the revision on merit considering the evidence and materials on record. 

 16. Moreover, I carefully examined the documents proved by both the parties. The sole basis of plaintiffs title is dakhila dated 10-10-1950 BS (Exhibits 2 and 6), which is an old document without any date and specification of land. Most of the rent receipts (Exhibits 3 and 5 series ) of plaintiffs are not relate to suit land. The documents (Exhibits) indicates that CS plot No. 962 is within the acquired land of LA Case No. 11 of 1921-22. Therefore, the observations made by Court of appeal below to that effect is not correct. It appears that earlier record of rights of plaintiffs were rescinded by Government in different Misc. cases. Now the suit land stands in the name of the Government (Exhibits Z-Z-1, Z-2) 

 17. It is significant that the suit was instituted on 18-11-2002 but prior to that i.e. on 21-3-1992 the suit land came under Government which was not challenged by plaintiffs. However, the learned Counsel for opposite-parties candidly submits that at present record of rights stands in the name of Government which is now under challenge in a review petition before the Assistant Commissioner (Land) and to that effect I am of the view that before institution of instant suit title of plaintiffs were clouded, for which they failed to seek their redress in any manner whatsoever. So instant suit for permanent injunction is not maintainable. 

 18. It further appears that all the issues involved in suit have rightly been framed, considered and decided by trial Court with reference to evidences and materials on record. Moreover, I do not find any misreading or non-consideration of evidence on record. The impugned judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below in its entirety are not well founded in the facts and circumstances of the case. So the ground urged and contentions advanced by learned Counsel for petitioners are correct exposition of law and facts and, as such, the legal pleas taken by him prevails and appears to have a good deal of force. On the contrary I failed to discover any merit in the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for opposite-parties. 

 Office is directed to send down the records of the case at once with a copy of judgment for information and necessary action.

Eshaque Ali ------Petitioner
Vs.
Aitunessa & ors ------Opposite parties
full_judgment:
3. The case of the plaintiff-opposite party Nos. 1-3, in short, was that an area of 1.01 acres of C.S. plot No. 195 appertaining to khewat No.I 92 originally belonged to Faizuddin in -/2/- annas share, Hachenuddin in -/4/-share, Maju Bibi in, /4/- annas share, Wahed in -2/- annas share and Tarapuddin in remaining -/4/-annas share. Tarapuddin died leaving 3 daughters viz, Amiron, Maiman and Rahimjan. Maiman and Rahimjan sold their shares to Hachenuddin by kabala, dated 3rd Ashar 1321 B.S. Amirjan sold her share to Hashem Ali and Tazem Ali by kabala. dated 29th Magh 1322 B.S. Hashem Ali and Tazem sold the same to Hachenuddin by kabala, dated 30th Sraban 1327 B.S. The share of Wahed developed upon Faizuddin by way of inheritance. Hachenuddin married Khatejan. Faizuddin died leaving behind 4 sons, viz, Kadam Ali, Rahman Ali, Karam Ali and Yakub Ali. Thus Hachenuddin got 8 annas share, Kadam Ali (defendant No.3) got -/1/- annas share, Nowab Ali got -/2/- annas share and Khatejan got -/2/- annas share. During the R.S. operation the aforesaid shares were correctly recorded. Hachenuddin and Khatejan died leaving one son, Kashem Ali and one daughter, plaintiff No. 3 Kashem Ali died leaving sister plaintiff No.3 and 2 wives, plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2, Kadam Ali died leaving 2 sons, defendant Nos. 5 and 6, 3 daughters, defendant Nos 7,8 and 9 and widow defendent No. 15, Nawab Ali died leaving 1 widow, 4 sons and 1 daughter, defendant Nos. 10-12 and 22-24. Thus the plaintiffs got -/10/- annas share in the 'Ka' schedule property and have been possessing the same. 

 4. During the S.A operation the land was wrongly recorded in the name of the defendant No. 1 Government of Bangladesh as khas land. On the basis of erroneous record of rights, the defendant No. 13 and Hashem Ali, the predecessor of defendant Nos. 14-21 took pattan of some portion of the suit land from the defendant No. 1 and created some collusive and fraudulent papers. In fact neither the defendant No. 1 nor the defendant Nos. 13-21 have any right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. The defendant No. I never auction purchased the suit land and never made the suit land khas. The Touzi of the suit land had never been sold in auction and defendant No. 1 never purchased the touzi and the under tenure of the Touzi had never been annulled and defendant No. 1 never brought the suit land under its khas possession and defendant No. 1 never in duo ted the defendant No. 13 and Hashem Ali into the possession of the suit land. The defendants in the month of Falgoon, 1381 B.S. claimed title to the suit land and the plaintiffs for the first time, came to know about the erroneous S.A. khatian. As the plaintiffs title to the suit land has been clouded, the suit has been filed. 

 5. The defendant No. 1, Government of Bangladesh contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable in the present form and it is barred by section 42 of Specific Relief Act. The suit land has rightly been recorded in the name of Government in khas No. 1. 

 6. The defendant No. 13 also contested the suit by filing another written statement denying the plaintiffs' right, title and interest in the suit laud, He has contended that the Touzi No. 7309 of Bakerganj Collect orate was sold in auction in Revenue Sale Case No. 199/49-50 and the Government auction purchased the Touzi and annulled all the encumbrances and, as such the Nim-Howla right of the predecessors of the plaintiffs was extinguished and the land was brought under khas possession of the Government and accordingly the land has been correctly recorded in the name of the Government. The further case of the defendant No. 13 was that he and his brother Hashem Ali took settlement of 0.16 acres of land appertaining to C. S. khatian No. 4430 in karsha right and has been possessing the same and that land has been correctly recorded in S.A khatian No. 3866. The defendant No.1 leased out 90 accrues of suit plot No. 179 to defendant No. 13 and his brother in Settlement Case No. 134 of 1968-69. Since the date of their lease the defendant No. 13 and his brothers have been possessing the suit land. The plaintiffs have no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. Hence the suit land is liable to be dismissed. 

 7. The [earned Munsif on consideration of evidence on record found that the plain-tiffs have failed to prove their right, title, interest and possession in the suit land and as such by his judgment and decree, dt. 23.4.80, dismissed the suit on contest against defendant Nos. 1 & 13 and ex parte against the rest without cost. 

 I have gone through the judgments of 'the Courts below and perused the evidence on record. 

 On consideration of evidence on record, the appellate court, has further found that the suit land appertains to Touzi No. 7309 and the said Touzi was sold in Revenue Sale Case No. 199/49-50 and Government auction purchased the same. 

 10. The only question arises now for our consideration is that whether the Nim-Howla interest of the plaintiffs was annulled by the Government. The Nim-Howla interest of the plaintiffs is an encumbrance which is not, ipso-facto, annulled by the Revenue Sale, but it is annulable at the option of the purchaser. The purchaser may annul an under tenure by institution of a suit or by any other suitable means. In this case, the Government neither instituted any suit for annulling the Nim-Howla interest of the plaintiffs nor issued any notice upon the plaintiffs asking them to vacate the suit land. The Government did not take possession of the land and there is no evidence on record to show that the Government by an unequivocal act indicated its intention to avoid the Nim-Howla interest of the plaintiffs. Cons daring all these facts and circumstances of the case, the appellate Court arrived ar the finding that "There is no overt act on the part of the purchaser-Government, which will show Government's intention to avoid the under-tenure of the plaintiffs. There is nothing to show that the Government ever took delivery of possession of the suit Nim-Howla." 

 11. Mr. Hemayetuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioners submitted that after the auction purchase, the suit land was recorded as khas land of the Government in the S.A. khatian and the land has been leased out to the defendant No. 13 and the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 14-21 by the Government and as such the appellate Court erred in holding that the Nim-Howla interest of the plaintiffs was not annulled. 

 12. The plaintiff's case is that they were not aware of the auction sale and the record of rights in the name of Government is wrong and without any basis whatsoever. I have gone through the written statement filed by the defendant No. I, the Government of Bangladesh, but I did not find there in any statement to suggest the purchaser-Government ever annulled the Nim-Howla interest of the plaintiffs after the auction purchase. The record of the Revenue Sale Case No. 199 of 1949-50 had been produced before the trial court and proved by D.W. 1 Sikdar A. Mannan. I have also gone through the said Revenue Sale record and I did not find anything in the record to show that the Nim-Howla interest of the plaintiffs was ever annulled or possession of the suit land taken by the Government. D.W. 1 Sikder A. Mamma, a Surveyor in the Estate Acquisition Department, has admitted in his cross-examination that the Government did not file any paper to show that possession was taken on the basis of the Revenue Sale. He has further stated that the Government has no paper to show that it (Government) delivered possession to the lessees after the alleged settlement. So.on consideration of the evidence, oral and documentary, the appellate Court has recorded the following finding with regard to the possession of the suit land:— 

 14. On consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, 1 find that the auction purchaser Government never annuled the Nim-Howla interest of the plaintiffs and never took possession of the suit land, and that by way of settlement from the Government the defendant No. 13 (the petitioner) and the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 14-21 did not possess the suit land. There is no illegality in the decision of the appellate court occasioning any failure of justice:

full_judgment:
D.C. Bhattacharya, J.-This appeal by special leave is against a judgment of a Bench of the High Court Division, setting aside, in exercise of the powers under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an order made by the first Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca, rejecting the prayer of the respondent for amendment of the additional written statement filed by the said respondent in a suit instituted by the appellants for declaration of their title. 

 2. The appellants instituted the suit as plaintiffs on 26-10-67 in the first Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca against Bangladesh, the respondent for declaration of their title to the land in suit and also for declaration that a certain notice, issued by the Member, Board of Revenue, upon the plaintiffs and all subsequent actions taken by him were illegal, void and without jurisdiction on the allegations that the suit land was originally the khas land of Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate which settled the same in 1344 B.S. with some of the plaintiffs processors and others in raiyati right, that during the survey operation under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the suit land was wrongly recorded in the name of the respondent, whereupon an application was filed on behalf of the appellants for correction of the record of rights under section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, that the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Dacca recognised them as the tenants on the basis of their settlement and long standing possession and realized rent from them, but that the Board of Revenue, by a notice dated 15-6- 67 purported to cancel the recognition already granted to the plaintiffs and their predecessors. 

 The respondent moved the High Court Division against the said order of rejection of the prayer for amendment, the additional written statement under section 115 of the Cede, upon which a rule was issued and the learned Judges by their judgment dated 5-7-73 made the rule absolute and allowed the respondent's application for amendment of the additional written statement on the view that the proposed amendment of the additional written statement would help the determination of the real question in controversy between the parties. 

 7. Special leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division was within its jurisdiction in interfering with the order of the Subordinate Judge in exercise of its power under section 115 of the Cede. 

 8. Mr. Akram Hossain Amin, learned Counsel appearing for the appellants, has contended that the power of amendment which the trial Judge possesses under Order 6, rule 17 of the Code is discretionary and that the learned Subordinate Judge having exercised his discretion to refuse the amendment en the view that the amendment would have the effect of deleting the defendant's admission in the pleading and would thereby prejudice the right of the plaintiffs, the learned Judges of the High Court Division exceeded their jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure in interfering with the discretion of the trial Judge in the exercise of which he had the necessary jurisdiction, 

 9. The power of amendment which has been conferred by the provision of Order 6, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure upon a Court has been expressed in the following words. 

 "The Court may at any stage of the proceedings allow either party to alter or amend his pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be just, and all such amendments shall be made, as may be necessary, for the purpose of determining the real questions in controversy between the parties." 

 10. It will appear that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge misdirected himself in approaching the question of justifiability of the amendment from a wrong point of view. It appears from his order that his refusal was dictated by the consideration that the defendant by the amendment was trying to get out of its admission and that the plaintiffs being deprived of the advantage of such an admission would be prejudiced. This consideration, which impelled the learned Subordinate Judge to refuse the amendment as has been referred to above, is absolutely irrelevant. The Court concerned shall have to find out, according to the terms of the rule whether the proposed amendment is likely to facilitate the determination of the real questions in controversy. The main dispute in the suit appears to arise from the averments of the plaintiffs on the one hand that they had acquired right, title and interest in respect of the disputed land by virtue of the alleged settlement granted by the original proprietors, namely, Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate, and the averments of the defendant, on the other hand, that there was no such settlement by the Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate in favour of some of the plaintiffs or their predecessors and seems others. The real question of controversy seems to be the creation or existence of the right, title and interest of the plaintiffs in respect of the disputed land by virtue of the said settlement. 

 The power of amendment of pleadings as provided in Order 6, rule 17 of the Code is certainly a matter of discretion but the court shall have to exercise such discretion judicially in conformity with the terms of the aforesaid provision. If the learned Subordinate Judge failed to exercise his discretion to allow the amendment of the written statement from absolutely a wrong point of view it would certainly by a failure on his part to exercise the jurisdiction as was conferred upon him by the aforesaid provision of Order 6, rule 17 of the Code. The learned Judges of the High Court Division appear to have taken the correct review in the matter and rightly exercised their revisional jurisdiction in setting aside the order of the learned Subordinate Judge.

full_judgment:
2. It is stated in the application that in LA Case No. 33 of 1958-59 several acres of land were purported to have been requisitioned for the Master Plan of Gulshan Model Town and in that LA Case the CS Plot Nos. 24, 25, 26, 42 and 43 measuring more or less 4.79 acres of land were also included. It is the specific case of the petitioners that they became the owners of the suit land by virtue of several registered deeds and since then they have been possessing the same and before them their predecessors-in-interest also possessed the suit land. It is their further case that since for about last 37 years land in question remained unused for which it was allegedly acquired, the acquisition in question was not acted upon and the aforesaid land was not required for the purpose for which it was acquired. Since 1984 there was consistent policy of the Government that the unused acquired land for a long period would be returned to the owners even without consulting the requiring body and in pursuance of that policy of the Government several hundreds of acres of land in different areas, which were not used for the purpose, were directed to be returned to the original owners and, as such, the petitioners being the owners of the land are entitled to get back the aforesaid land in question as the same remained unused for last 37 years. 

 3. It is the case of Respondent No. 4, the Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakkha that in LA Case No. 33 of 1958-59 the land in question was taken over by RAJUK by Gazette Notification for the purpose of the Master Plan of Gulshan Model Town and since the land in question vested to RAJUK and RAJUK is the owner since Gazette Notification dated 23-6-60, the property in question cannot be returned to the owners. It was the further case of respondent No. 4 that the original owners were given compensation and, as such, they had no right to transfer the same to the present petitioners. Since the present petitioners are purchasers in the year 1989, they had no locus standi to file the writ petition inasmuch as the property vested to the requiring body RAJUK in the year 1960. 

 5. This information was asked from the Deputy Commissioner by the Ministry in pursuance of the letter of the petitioner vide Annexure-H(I). Annexure-H(3) is the copy of the map of the area in question. Annexure-H (4) is the copy of the two Gazette notifications by which it was shown that in LA Case No. 63/1959-60 the unused land had been returned to the former owners of the land vide Gazette notification dated 29th November, 1993 and also in the Gazette notification dated 29 December, 1993 with regard to LA Case No. 63/1959-60 the unused lands were returned. Both were published in the Bangladesh Gazetee on 2nd December, 1993. In reply to the Ministry the Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA), Dhaka, informed the Government that in the relevant section of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA) no papers were available with regard to this acquisition of SA and CS Plot Nos. 24, 25, 26, 42 and 43 in the Samir Mouza. The land in question was under water at the relevant time and it was found that the suit land was under possession of the owners M Mohsin and others and this RAJUK did not take any step for returning the same to the owners. It was further replied that Plot Nos. 24, 25, 26, 42 and 43 of Samir Mouja was acquired by RAJUK vide LA Case No. 33/1958-59 and Gazette Notification was published on 23-6-60. It was also seen that the possession was taken by the RAJUK on 4-8-59 and 21-9-60. Further, it was reported that CS Plot Nos. 24, 25, 26, 42 and 43 of Samir Mouja and Plot No. 87 of Mohakhali Mouja were not acquired and the papers and documents of the aforesaid two moujas were not available in the LA Office. Further, it was stated from the office of the LA Collector that though the Gazette Notification dated 23-6-60 was published, no document was available with regard to taking over possession of the aforesaid plots by the requiring body. The lands in question were low lands and the same was under possession of the owners, namely, Mr Mohsin and others. 

 6. In the affidavit-in-reply the petitioners have filed a letter dated 30th October, 1984 issued by the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms. It was addressed to the Secretary, Ministry of Works. In this letter the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms expressed their views that the lands which were purportedly acquired but not used by the requisitioning authority till today should be given back to the owners and the same cannot be kept unused for an indefinite period. The decision as well as the principles enunciated by the Government that if it is found that in spite of acquisition the land in question remained unused for indefinite period and for a long time the same should be released in favour of the owners even without referring the matter to the requiring body. On the basis of the aforesaid decision, of the Government a circular was issued on 22-5-86 by the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms. This circular is very important for the purpose of the present case. In the circular it was categorically stated that the purported acquired land, the possession of which has not yet been taken by the requiring body, should be returned to the owners. Even in the case of failing to pay the full compensation the Deputy Commissioner will also be authorised to take back those lands from the requiring body. 

 7. Further, it was decided that in cases where the owners of the unused lands applied for getting back their lands, the Deputy Commissioner shall give a report on such lands and the same with comments the Deputy Commissioner should return to the Ministry for its consideration. The circular of the Government dated 22-5-86 is Annexure X(I). Annexure-X(2) is the rent receipt wherein the rent of the land in question was paid by Md Abdul Mannan for a sum of Taka 1,947.00. It was paid on 31-12-89. Annexure-X(2) also bears the name of Md Abdul Mannan. The mutation was made on 8-11-89 in respect of the suit land. Annexure-X(3) also shows payment of rent. Annexure-X series futher show several rent receipts and also mutation of the name of Md Shahjahan vide Mutation Case No. 406 dated 7-1-88. These rent receipts vide Annexure-X(4) series show payment of rent for the disputed lands for several other years and a duplicate carbon receipt is also annexed in the name of Mohsin Housing Commercial Complex which is a proprietorship business of M Mohsin Hossain, one of the petitioners before this Court. Another annexure shows the name of Mohsin Hossain mutated in the record of rights vide Mutation Case No. 1330/1989-90 dated 5-2-90. Annexure-X(5) series show that payment of rent by Mrs Masuma Khan with the DCR dated 6-2-90. The mutation was also made in the name of Mrs Masuma Khan vide Mutation Case No. 1331 of 1989-90 dated 5-2-90. Annexure-X(6) shows that the petitioners prayed to the District Adjutant of Ansar and VDP for giving whole-time guards for the petitioner''s property on the ground that some unauthorised persons were threatening to come over and illegally occupy the suit lands. 

 10. Mr Rafiqul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that though on paper it was allegedly shown that the suit area was purported to have been acquired for the master plan of Gulshan Model Town, yet it was not, in fact, acted upon for last 37 years. It is his case that it was the provision of law that within two weeks from the date of requisition the possession should be taken over. But in the instant case for last 37 years possession was not taken over by the Government. He has further submitted that the petitioners have annexed so many papers and documents, as discussed above, in order to show their continuous possession of the suit property. On the other hand he submits that the respondents, particularly, respondent No. 4 failed to show by producing any documents before this Court that the possession was taken over by the RAJUK and they are maintaining the possession since 1960. It is submitted that only a Gazette Notification was shown that the land in question was acquired in 1960. Excepting that, with regard to the taking over possession and also with regard to payment of compensation, the respondents failed to produce any paper or document before this Court. 

 16. It is further submitted that the decision taken by the Government by the resolution of the inter-ministerial meeting in 1984 and the subsequent letters of the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms and further the circular issued by the Government in 1986 as referred to above clearly show that the Government had taken decision in respect of all the acquired but unused lands in this country. The Government took a decision that if it is found that the lands purportedly acquired was not used for a long time for the said purpose they should be given back to the owners even without the consent or consulting the requiring body. The petitioners have annexed several documents to show that in pursuance of this decision of the Government as well as the circular issued subsequently several hundreds of unused lands which were purportedly acquired earlier were directed to be released in favour of the previous owners by issuing Gazette Notification. Mr Huq submits that since this is the policy/decision of the Government since 1984 and since this policy decision is applicable to all cases of the country with regard to unused lands though acquired earlier and since the decision of the Government had been acted upon in several case, such policy decision of the Government should also be applicable in the case of present petitioners in view of the fact that admittedly the suit lands remained unused for last 37 years though purportedly RAJUK acquired it for the master plan of Gulshan Model Town. Further, he submits that even the plan itself shows that the land in question remained outside the Gulshan Model Town Master Plan till today and there was no Gazette Notification in pursuance of sections 73 and 74 of the Town Improvement Act for amendment or further extension of the Gulshan Model Town Master Plan. Mr Huq submits that in the present case the general policy decision of the Government should also be applicable. We find force in the above contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioners. He further submits that taking advantage of law or by misreading the provision of law the authority cannot deprive the citizens of this country of their proprietary right. 

 17. Mr Huq further submits that since this overall policy of the Government initiated from the year 1984 and since in the meantime it was acted upon and in several acquisition cases the unused lands were given back to the original owners, the petitioners should not be an exception of that. Mr Huq has further drawn our attention to Articles 27, 31 and 42 of the Constitution, namely, the fundamental rights of the citizens. Article 27 provides that all citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law. Article 31 provides that to enjoy the protection of the law, and to be treated in accordance with law, and only in accordance with law, is the inalienable right of every citizen, wherever he may be, and of every other person for the time being within Bangladesh, and in particular no action detrimental to the life, liberty, body, reputation or property of any person shall be taken except in accordance with law. Article 42 provides that subject to any restrictions imposed by law, every citizen shall have the right to acquire, hold, transfer or otherwise dispose of property, and no property shall be compulsorily acquired , nationalised or requisitioned save by authority of law. Mr Huq submits that considering the above the Government had taken the overall policy of releasing the unused lands purportedly acquired earlier in favour of the owners. 

 18. He further submits that since policy of the Government had been acted upon and the unused land in several LA Cases had already been released in favour of the owners, the petitioners are entitled to get back their lands in view of the provisions of Article 27, 31 and 42 of the Constitution. We find force in the above submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners. Since taking advantage of certain law the authority had violated the rights of the present petitioners guaranteed under the Constitution as stated above and since the land in question though acquired kept unused for long 37 years, we are of the view that definitely such an action of the authority offended the fundamental rights, namely, Articles, 27, 31 and 42 of the Constitution. In this view of the matter, we find that the claim of the present petitioners should succeed. 

 19. Mr Rafiqul Huq has referred before us the Administrative Law, International Student Edition, by HWR Wade and CF Forsyth, at 418 regarding Inconsistency and Unfairness Legitimate Expectation. He submits that the petitioners have got the legitimate expectation in view of the fact that in pursuance of the overall policy for giving back the unused acquired lands to the previous owners, every person in the country whose property was allegedly acquired but kept unused for such unusual longer period, can expect that his property should be returned to him otherwise there will be discrimination between citizen and citizen. It is provided in that book that : "Inconsistency of policy may also amount to an abuse of discretion, particularly, when undertaking or statement of intent are disregarded unfairly or contrary to citizen''s legitimate expectation. The Privy Council, in holding that the Government of Hong Kong must honour its public understanding to treat its deportation case on its merit, had applied the principles that a public authority is bound by its understanding." 

 "If the published policy was to be changed, the applicant should be given full and serious consideration whether there is some ever riding public interest justifying tiler new departure "Courts now expect the Government Departments to honour their statements of policy or intention or else to treat the citizen with the fullest personal consideration. Unfairness in the form of unreasonableness is clearly allied to unfairness by violation of natural justice. It was in the latter context that the doctrine of legitimate expectation was invented, but it is now providing to be a source of substantive as well as of procedural rights, Lord Scarman has stated emphatically that unfairness in the purported exercise of power can amount to an abuse or excess of power, and this may become an important general doctrine." 

 "The argument under the label ''estoppel'' and the ''legitimate expectation'' arguments are substantially the same. In this conflict of doctrines the demands of fairness are proving the stronger. But those demands cannot be pressed to the point where they obstruct changes of policy which a Government should be at liberty to make within its discretionary powers, or legitimate practices such as selective prosecution of tax offenders by the Inland Revenue". It further provides that in the same way the Court of Appeal held that the public authority has a duty to act with fairness and consistency in its dealings with the public, and that if it makes inconsistent decisions unfairly or unjustly it misuses its powers. 

 21. Mr Hasan Arif further submits that the present petitioners have no locus standi to file this writ petition in view of the fact that they are not the original owners of the suit land and after acquisition the original owners had no legal right to transfer the same to the present petitioners. It is difficult for us to accept the above submission of Mr Hasan Arif in view of the fact that by registered transfer deeds the present petitioners have become the successors of the original owners and if the original owners are entitled to challenge this acquisition proceedings definitely the present petitioners being successors- in-interest have got the locus standi to challenge the acquisition in question. Since by the registered deeds the land in question was transferred to the present petitioners and since the names of the predecessors-in-interest of the petitioners were recorded in the record of the rights and since the names of the present petitioners were also mutated in the record of rights and since then they have been all along paying the rents to the Government in respect of the suit land, it shows that the predecessors-in-interest as well as the present petitioners have been continuing their possession in the suit property. Mr Hasan Arif has also raised some question in respect of the validity of the deeds in question. But this Court cannot go into the right and title of the predecessors-in-interest of the petitioners as well as the present petitioners in view of the fact that prima facie it shows that the predecessors- in-interest of the petitioners had transferred the suit lands to the present petitioners by registered instruments. As such, there is no scope for this Court to inquire and investigate into the allegation of Mr Hasan Arif. As such we find no substance in his contention. By transfer through valid registered deed, the petitioners stepped into the shoes of the original owners. Further, the title of the petitioners in the lands in question can only be challenged by the previous owners and nobody else. 

 22. Mr Hasan Arif further submits that the RAJUK has been taking steps for allotting as well as using the said property. Mr Rafiqul Huq submits that as back as from the year 1992 the present petitioners are trying to get the land released from the acquisition and they made several representations to different authorities for appropriate relief. Seeing the efforts of the present petitioners, now the RAJUK is claiming that they are taking steps to do something with regard to the suit property. Mr Huq submits that this is a malafide intention and they are trying to frustrate the purpose as well as the policy decision of the Government. Since it appears for us that the present petitioners have been possessing the suit land and since they are trying to get their land released from acquisition, it is difficult for us to hold that the RAJUK is doing something for extension of the master plan of Gulshan Model Town. As the lands in question are still under the possession of the petitioners and as there was no Gazette Notification showing the amendment for inclusion of the suit lands in question under the master plan of Gulshan Model Town, we are of the view that the claim of the learned Advocate for respondent No. 4 is absolutely baseless and it is now being made only to frustrate the purpose of the present petitioners case. In this view of the matter, we do not find substance in the submissions of Mr Hasan Arif. 

 23. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the legal position as well as the Government decision and policy as discussed above and also considering the papers and documents annexed with the Writ Petition and affidavit-in-reply as discussed above, we are of the view that this Writ Petition should succeed and the petitioners should get proper relief as prayed for. 

 24. In the result, this Rule is made absolute and let the petitioners continue their possession in the suit lands as they are continuing for last 37 years. The respondents are directed to release the suit lands, namely, SA Plot Nos. 24, 25, 26, 42 and 43 of Mouza Samir Police Station Tejgaon now Gulshan, District Dhaka measuring 4.79 acres of land from LA Case No. 33/1958-59 as unused lands in favour of the petitioners immediately.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 27 of 1980
lawyer:
Mr. Marfat Ali---For the Appellant. 
Mr. Moazzem Hossain, D.A.G---For the respondent.
parties:
Fazlur Rahman ------ Appellant.
Versus
People's Republic of Bangladesh ------Respondent.
full_judgment:
3. Defendant No. 1, People's Republic of Bangladesh and defendant No. 2, A.D.C. (Rev), contested the suit by filing a joint written statement. Their case, in brief, is that an area of 80.86 acres of land including the suit land belonged to Zaminders Ranjit Singh Nahar and others and the said lands were recorded in khatian No. 3 in mouza Nafanagar within P.S. Bochegeni in District Dinajpur. The said lands were sold in auction No. 26.4.63 in Certificate Case No. 22 of 1962-63 and was purchased by the Government, who got possession of the same. It is seated by the defendants that plain-tiffs father had a jama for 0.83 acre (schedule B land) at a rental of Tk.1/1-and the land was recorded in the name of the plaintiffs father in khatian No. 11. Plaintiffs father paid rent up to 1369 B.S. Subsequently in collusion with some employees of the Tahasil Office plaintiff caused overwriting in Karcha Book, changed the page of R.O.R. and Register-11 showing amalgamation of the jama of Tk. 1 /1- of Khatian No. 11 and made an amalgamated jama of Tk. 15/1/- in respect of the said land. The plaintiff has illegally tampered with P.R.R., R.O.R. and Karcha Book and other Registers and papers of the settlement offices and he did so in collusion with the employees of the Revenue Department. The defendants categorically assert that plaintiffs papers in respect of the land of schedule A to the plaint are forged concocted and vogue without creating any right, title and interest in his favour. The matter having been reported to the A.D.C. (Rev), he sent a notice to the plaintiff. Thereafter he perused the plaintiffs papers. examined Register-II and other relevant documents and registers of the Revenue Office and being satisfied about the forgery committed by the plaintiff in respect of the said amalgamated jama, under his order dated 8.9.77 restored plot Nos. 554, 694, 682, 500, 501. 474, 473, 472 and 544 to khatian No. 3 of the landlord by excluding the same from R.S. khatian No. 11 where these were entered through forgery and manipulation and maintained 0.83 in R. S. Khatian No. 11 in the name of the plaintiff. 

 4. At the trial court plaintiff examined six witnesses as against one by the defendants. Both sides have filed a number of documents in support of their respective cases. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence on record and 'examination of all papers filed by both sides came to the finding that the plaintiff failed to prove the settlement of the land of schedule A from the landlord, that P.W.4 Serajul Haque and other witnesses of the plaintiff could not be relied on and that the papers filed by the plaintiff were of recent origin created with an eye to the suit. With this finding the learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit. 

 5. Aggrieved by the judgment and decree the plaintiff has preferred this appeal. Mr. Marfat Ali, learned Advocate for the appellant has taken us through the pleadings the impugned judgment and decree and the evidence on record contending that the plaintiff has proved the document of pattan Ext. 1 (a), which is a chit dated 15 Chaitra. 1352 B.S. granted by the landlords Ran Singh Nahar and others to prove his settlement of the land of schedule A and that this pattani paper. Ext. 1 (a). is supported by dakhilas Ext. 2 and Ext. 2(b). granted by the Tahasildars of the land-lords. Mr. Marfat Ali has contended that the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error in failing to hold that the plaintiffs chit and dakhilas are genuine documents in support of his title to the suit property. The learned Advocate for the appellant has further submitted that plaintiffs dakhilas, Ext 2(c) dated 11.3.75 granted by the Government Tahashil and the P.R.R. and S.A. khatian in the name of the plaintiff should have been relied on by the trial court for decreasing the suit for declaration of tenancy right of the plaintiff under the government. 

 7. It is not disputed that plaintiffs father Mashiruddin took settlement from the ex-Land-lords Ranjit Singh Nahar and others the land of schedule B measuring 0.83 acre at a rental of Tk. 1/1 /- recorded in R.S. khatian No. 11. The dispute centers round the alleged story of pattan by the plaintiff in respect of the land of schedule A measuring 20.41 acres on the basis of a chit. Ext. 1(a). bearing the date 15 Chaitra, 1352 B.S. Plaintiff has examined some witnesses in order to prove the story of settlement of the land of schedule A to the plaint. In his evidence as P.W.1 plaintiff Fazlur Rahman states that his father took pattan of 0.83 acre (schedule B) at a rental of Tk. 1/1/- on the basis of a chit and that he himself got settlement of 20.41 acres (schedule A) at a jama of Tk. 14/- and he has filed two chits said to have been granted by Narendra Chatarjee, Naib of the ex-landlord. Plaintiff himself was present when the said chit, Ext. 1 (a). was granted and he got settlement of the land of schedule A on the basis of this pattan. This witness has also filed 3 dakhilas and claims to have made the land fit for cultivation. P.W. 4 Serajul Haque states that he was a Tahasildar of the Zaminder and he states that Narendra Chatarjee, Nail) of the Zaminder, wrote the chit, dated 12 Falgoon, 1350 B.S. (Ext. l) in respect of 0.83 acre of land in the name of plaintiffs father and that the said Naib also wrote a chit. Ext. 1 (a), in respect of 20.41 acres at a jama of Tk. 14/-. P.W.4 Serajul Haque, wrote dakhila, Ext. 2(a), in respect of 0.83 acre of land in the name of plaintiffs father and also granted dakhila Ext. 2 in respect of 20.41 acres in the name of the plaintiff. P.W.4 further states that the dakhila, Ext. 2(b) in respect of 20.41 acres in the name of the plaintiff is in the handwriting of Bhupati Chowdhury, who was the Zamindar's Taltasildar before him. In cross-examination the defendants challenged that P.W.4 Serajul Haque was in the employment of the Jamindar as a Tahasildar or that Bhupati Chowdhury was ever employed by the Zamindar as a Tahasildar. It was further challenged in the cross-examination of this witness that Narendra Chataijee was employed as Naib. P.W.4 has, in fact, failed to show any paper or document showing that he was the landlord's Tahasildar at any time or that Bhupati or Narendra Chatarjee were ever employed by the landlords as a Tahasildar or Naib. The other witnesses supporting the plaintiffs story of settlement is P.W.5 Kalu Mohammad who claims to have been present at the time of taking of pattan by the plaintiff. In his cross-examination, P.W.5 Kalu Mohammad states that he cannot say the plot number or area of the suit land. He claims that he went to the landlord's Sheresta in the morning by train but he can-not say the time of the train. The learned Deputy Attorney General has challenged the veracity of these two witnesses to supporting plaintiffs story of pattan from the Zamindar. There is no doubt that these two witnesses, P.W.4 and P.W.5. have not been able to prove plaintiffs story of pattan satisfactorily. 

 11. Ext. 4(a) is certified copy of an order dated 8.9.77 passed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev), Dinajpur, in case No. 71/27 of 1976-77 under rule 23(4) of the Tenancy Rules made under section 152 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 1950. The present plaintiff was opposite party in this proceeding and he filed his pattani papers including dakhilas alleged to have been granted by the ex-landlords. In his order the A.D.C. (Rev) mentions that the first set of dakhilas showing settlement of 0.83 acres at a rental of Tk.1.06 by the ex-landlord appears to be genuine, but the second set of dakhilas showing settlement of 20.14 acres at a rental of Tk.14/- appears to be forged and produced recently. On examination the A.D.C. (Rev) found that S.A. Khatian No. 11 in respect of 0.83 acre of land was rightly recorded in favour of the opposite party but subsequently through manipulation 20.14 acres of land of different plots were brought into that khatian by increasing the rent to Tk. 15/-. On examination by the A.D.C (Rev). Registrar-II showed signs of manipulation by overwriting. The P.R.R. and Tahasil the copy of S.A. Khatian were examined and it was found that nine plots of khas land were included in Khatian No. 11 with different ink. It was further noted that though the opposite party (present plaintiff) paid rent for the khatian at the rate of Tk. 1.06 up to 1369 B.S. yet after this manipulation rent was again realised from him for the same holding from 1367 B.S. to 1370 B.S. On examination of the Office copy of the S.A. khatian of the C.O. (Rev) it was found that vanishing ink was used to erase those plots from the khas khatian and that handwriting of khatian No. 11 (disputed khatian) was entirely different from the handwriting of khatian Nos. 10 and 12. The A.D.C. (Rev) found Khatian No. 11 in the name of the opposite party (present plaintiff) which contains 0.83 acre at a rental of 11.1.06 but subsequently through fraud khas land measuring 20.14 acres of 9 plots were brought in Khatian No. 11 and accordingly plot Nos. 554, 694. 682. 500, 501, 474, 473, 472 and 554 fraudulently entered into khatian No. 11 were restored to Khatian No. 3 maintaining 0.83 acre of land in the name of the plaintiff in khatian No. 11 under rule 23 (4) the State Acquisition Rule. Under rule 23(4) the Revenue Officer is empowered to direct excision of fraudulent entry from the record of rights after final publication there of after consulting the previous settlement records, preliminary rent-rolls, draft record-of-rights. tahasil copies of records and Register-II. 

 father. It is clear from the evidence on record that the chit Ext. 1 (a) bearing the date 15 Chaitra, 1352 B.S. and dakhilas, Ext, 2 and 2(b). are forged and fabricated papers. In fact, we find no basis for the alleged story of pattan in respect of the land of schedule A to the plaint. Plaintiff has, however, managed to secure a dakhilas Ext. 2 (c) from the Government Tahasil Office. But this paper as well as the P.R.R. and S.A. Khatian in respect of the suit land are of no consequence as those have been secured by the plaintiff in collusion with the employees of the Revenue Department.

parties:
