2. The plaintiffs Respondents petitioners filed Title Suit No. 35 of 1999 against the Defendant Appellant-Opposite party No. 1 for declaration of title to and khas possession of the suit land. The plaintiffs stated that the suit jote of the scheduled lands situated under Mouza Khankhanapur, PS and District Rajbari in RS Khatian No.419 and SA Khatian No. 464 belonged to a family of owners in possession consisting of Amir Mridha, Mohiuddin Mridha, Khatoon Jahiran Bibi and Amena Khatoon who as RS recorded tenants hold the lands in ejmali. It transpired that the co-sharer tenant Amir Mridha died unmarried leaving behind his brother Mohiuddin Mridha, sisters Hazu Khatoon and Jahiran Bibi, and mother Amena Khatoon as his nears and successors. Hazu Khatoon and Jahiran Bibi sold 97 decimals and 13 decimals of land to their brother Mohiuddin on 12-2-1949 by registered Kabala and handed over possession to him. Mohiuddin Mridha sold 30 decimals of land which Mohiuddin got by inheritance through registered Kabala on 14-10-1950 to Shandari Nessa wife of Nazar Ali Pramanik and handed over the possession of the same to her Shandari Nessa possessing 30 decimals of lands through her husband Nazar Ali Pramanik died before the SA Operation leaving her only son Abdul Khaleque Pramanik and her husband Nazar Ali Pramanik as her heirs and successors. Upon Nazar Ali's death, Abdul Khaleque Pramanik inherited his father's share later selling his lands to Shushil Kumar Bhokta through registered kabala on 14-2-1975 only to buy back Shushil Kumar's lands through registered kabala on 18-2-1978. Subsequently, Abdul Khaleque Pramanik being the owner in possession of the lands sold the same on 18-2-1993 by kabala Deed No. 8817 registered on 18-12-1993 to the plaintiff Nos. 1-2 and handed over possession to them. It is against this backdrop that the Defendant filed Title suit No. 155 of 1990 which was dismissed for default. The plaintiffs filed case No. 30 of 1994 in the Union , Parishad against the Defendant No. 1 for having cut away bamboos from plot No. 5567 by force, thereafter taking possession of and erecting a house thereon, which was not contested by the Defendant and the plaintiffs got an ex parte order of compensation. The Defendant also forcibly took possession of some lands that were initially subject of a wrong entry in the BS records that was subsequently corrected in the plaintiffs" favour upon an objection filed by them That notwithstanding, the Defendant, thereafter proving unwilling to give up possession of the suit lands on, one plea or the other at the plaintiff's request and on 6-3-1999 the Defendant having refused to remove his house there from, the plaintiffs filed the Title suit praying for declaration of Title and for his possession. 

 7. It is against this backdrop that this Court, like the trial Court below, has had to consider the issue of dispossession raised by the petitioners as is said to have occurred on 5-5-1994. It is not disputed that the suit land was sold to the petitioners on 18-12-1993. The petitioners claim that soon thereafter the opposite party No. 1 actively dispossessed the petitioners constraining them to filed case No. 30 of 1994 with the concerned Union Parishad arbitration form praying for an for an order and direction on the opposite party No. 1 remove all obstacles to the petitioners possession of the land and to restore and compensate as necessary. It has been submitted by the learned Advocate for the Opposite party No.1 that this case was filed on 7-5-1994 and disposed of on 16-2-1995 without any notice to the opposite party No.1. The accuracy of this submission is suspect as relevant records of the proceedings as found in the Exhibit-3 series show that the opposite party No.1 having put in an appearance on 9-6-1994, thereafter, remained absent in the two years following the filing of the case leading thereby to an exparte disposal of the same on 16-2-1995 with the arbitration form having taken notice on 19-1-1995 of the sustained failure on the part of the opposite party No.1 to appear despite repeated notices. The order and direction given in that case on 16-2-1995 reads thus— 

 This order was found by the learned Assistant Judge to be in evidence of both the petitioner's possession of and dispossession from the suit land. A perusal of the Exhibit 3 documents pertaining to case No. 30 of 1994 reveals no ground for this Court to disagree with that finding by the learned Assistant Judge. The next stage of the legal battle was fought out in the petitioners Objection case No. 498 of 1995 challenging the earlier entry in the draft Record of rights of 1992 in favour of the opposite party No. 1. This case, as is evident in the Exhibit-4 judgment dated 2-11-1997, was filed under the relevant provisions of the state Acquisition Rules, 1951 read with those of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Proceeding on the disputed claims to the property by the petitioner and the opposite party No. 1 and referring to the history of litigation pertaining to the sale as evident in particular in Civil Case No. 155 of 1990, the judgment found against the correctness of the entry favour in the opposite party No. 1 in the draft Record of rights and found for entering the petitioners names instead. This in this Court view, also further bolstered the petitioners claims as adjudicate upon in case No. 30 of 1994. It is asserted, that an appeal as ostensibly preferred by the opposite party No. 1 against this judgment awaiting disposal, therefore, leading the opposite party No. 1 to question the very maintainability of the petitioners suit. This Court finds that the question of a pending appeal arises in the statement made by the opposite party No.1 upon cross-examination in somewhat vague terms and appears not to have been substantiated by evidence by the opposite party No. 1 of there before the trial Court or the lower appellate Court. This Court, upon a perusal of all relevant documents, finds that no attempt was made by the opposite party No. 1 to prove further the filing or the pendency of such appeal. 

 8. In light of the above, it is this Court's view that the trajectory of litigation pertaining to the disputed land, and as aptly appreciated by the learned Assistant Judge upon examining evidence, has been one of confirmation in various legal forums of the chain of title commencing in 1950 and continuing uninterruptedly to culminate in the acquisition of title by the petitioners in 1993. The issues of possession, title and dispossession that has loomed large in this case, have been settled in at least three different legal forums in Civil case No. 155 of 1990 case No. 30 of 1994 and objection case No. 498 of 1996 (Exhibits 2, 3 and 4 respectively). There is nothing on record that goes to show that in any such legal forum the title of the opposite party No. 1 by inheritance and gift was formally established on its own terms or with a view to dislodging in any way the claims to title and possessions put forward by the petitioners. 

 9. It is in this context that this Court is now laced with impugned judgment of the learned joint District Judge which in reversing the trial Court's judgment came to a finding, inter alia, that though the prima facts title of the petitioners predecessors in interests could be proven before the trial Court there is the outstanding question of actual and uninterrupted possession of the land by the petitioners which thereby proved fatal to the petitioners case at the appellant stage. It is not clear to this Court as to how and why the learned District Judge came to take issue with the question of possession, given the fact that the judgment of the trial Court amply discussed the issue and disposed of the same with an express finding upon a consideration of the evidence on record as corroborated by the PWs. That difficulty, in the view of this Court, stems primarily from the lack of discussion of evidence, oral and documentary, by the lower appellate Court to support its finding in this regard. In other words, that judgment is not ably served by definite and specific findings supported by reasoned consideration of evidence. In the absence of cogent reasoning or of clear findings on any issue of fact and law in the impugned judgment, this Court in revision has been hard pressed to best understand the correctness or general drift and gist of the impugned judgment. This Court finds that in that regard the impugned judgment fails far short of the standard in Order 41, rule XXXI of the Code. Considering the specificity of the findings of the trial Court based on full consideration of facts and evidence, this Court fails to see why the impugned judgment or reversal is so marked by its back of elaboration to any level of satisfaction of the reasons no reversing the trial Court's judgment. Moreover, and on the basis of this Court's reading of relevant facts, and oral and documentary evidence, this Court also finds that the learned joint District Judge came to an incorrect decision in reversing the trial Court's judgment. There is brother in the facts or evidence to show or justify the issue taken by the lower appellate Court with the Court with the petitioners possession or the lack of it of the suit land at all material times and their dispossession there from and in that regard, the learned joint District Judge is found to have erred in law in reaching an erroneous decision to reverse the trial Court's judgment. The learned joint District Judge failed to no to that the petitioners having been better able to prove their title and possession in the suit land as compared to the opposite party No.1 and that the trial Court properly and sufficiently adjudged the matter in favour of the petitioners. 

 Send down the Lower Court Records at once.

5. Further plaint case is that amongst the sons of Banku Bihar', Baidya Nath was the eldest and used to look after the entire property. During survey, he got the entire land recorded both in SA and RS Khatian in his name only. The plaintiffs along with defendant no. 1 Birendranath and defendant no.2 Kalipad Mondal all through were in joint possession. The suit land was never partitioned by metes and bounds. When in the month of July, 2000 demand for partition was refused for the last time, the plaintiff was constrained to institute the suit. 

 8. Defendant no. 1, I contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the plaint case. Ile claimed that his father Baidya Nath acquired the land of schedule `ka' with his own money and in his own interest and was in exclusive possession. Record of rights was prepared with the knowledge of both plaintiff and defendant no.2 who had got no right, title and/or possession in said land. The suit land was never joint and the plaintiff and/or defendant no.2 were never in joint possession. Some of the suit land was acquired and Baidya Nath received the compensation. Baidya Nath also gifted some land to the defendant no.3, Prolog Kumar Mondal and Mridul Rani Mondal. 

 20. The trial Court accordingly found that BankuBehari Mondal acquired the suit land with his money and in his interest but in the name of eldest minor son Baidya Nath. Defendant no. 3 as DW 2 also failed to prove exclusive possession of Baidya Nath as he found none to corroborate him. It also found that the deeds of gift dated 22.12.79, 03.05.99 and 18.06.89 were created in order to grab the land. Appellate Court also affirmed the findings of the trial Court on due consideration of the evidence on record. It also found that Baidya Nath as eldest son used to look after the land and got the land recorded in his name. Such wrong record of rights could not destroy the right and title of the plaintiff and defendant no. 2 in the suit land. 

 21. We have perused the record. The aforesaid conclusions are borne out by the record. Hence, no exception could be taken against such concurrent findings, which are now binding. 

 22. It also appears from the record that the property was never partitioned by metes and bound. The plaintiff and defendants were in joint possession of the suit land. PW 2 to 4 also supported the plaintiff, PW 1 on joint possession of the suit property. Defendant no. 2 as DW 1 supported the plaintiff case in toto. 

 Send down the records at once.

2. The petitioners as plaintiffs brought Title Suit No. 631/1 in the Court off Munsif Moralganj seeking reliefs as aforesaid. The plaint case, in brief, is that schedule land belonged to Olimuddin and Alimuddin, the two brothers. They settled 4.41 acres of land to Safaruddin Faraji, Alimuddin settled 2.71 acre of land to Olimuddin who died leaving a son Mahajuddin, daughter Laxmi Bibi and wife Shajal Bibi. During CS operation the said 2.71 acres of land was recorded in the name of Menhajuddsi and Laxmi Bibi in CS Khatian No. 689.Plaintiff No.Iisthe son of said Menhajuddin. The name of Safaruddin Faraji was recorded in CS Khatian No. 688 in respect of 4.41 acres and the said 2.71 acres of land was recorded in Khatian No. 689 in the name of the plaintiffs’ father and his Fufu maternal aunt as Kolkorsha. The plaintiffs father purchased the land of plot Nos. 1822 and 182412134 of CS Khatian No. 688 from Safaruddin Faraji and entered into possession and accordingly in the remark column of the said Khatian the possession of Menhajuddin as purchaser was recorded. Laxmi Bibi and Shajal Bibi gifted their portion of the property to Menhajuddin by the registered deeds of gift dated 14-6-1926 and put him in possession and Menhajuddin became the owner of the land of CS Khatian No. 689 and possessed the same. Thus Menhajuddin became the owner of the land measuring 2.71 acres in CS Khatian No. 689 by dint of and also by inheritance and he acquired title in the land to the extent of 0.92 decimals comprising plot No. 1822 and 1824/2134 of CS Khatian No. 688 and thus Menhajuddin became the owner of the suit land measuring 3.63 acres and had been in possession of the same. The plaintiff No.1 further pleaded that for nonpayment of rent by the under tenants of CS Khatian No. 688 under original CS Khatian No. 687 and the heirs of Alimuddin having 8 annas share in the CS Khatian No. 687 having failed to pay rent for their portion of the land, the landlord brought Rent suit for realization of arrear rent and in execution of the rent decree the land of the said Khatian was auction sold which was purchased in the benami of Asmat Ali Howlader the maternal uncle of the plaintiff with the money of the plaintiff given by the defendant No. 19 and that Asmat Ali the predecessor of the defendants Nos. 1-14 had not paid the bid money for the auction purchase. It is the case of the plaintiff that after the auction purchase the plaintiff did not get possession in the land as the under tenancy which is an encumbrance against the certificate purchase had not been annulled according to the provision of Bengal Tenancy Act. The plaintiff further averred that during the plaintiffs minority the said maternal uncle managed the auction purchased land and the rent was paid in the name of Asmat Ali who is the benamder of the plaintiff. The plaintiffs’ father possessed the suit land as mentioned in schedule Kha during his life time. By amicable settlement amongst the co-owners the plaintiff became the absolute owner of the suit land and he has been possessing the land sometimes cultivating by his own labour and sometimes by borgaders for more than 12 years. During the SA and RS settlement operation the name of Asmat Ali Howlader was recorded as per advice of the plaintiff. After the death of Asmat Ali the defendant Nos. 1-12 the successors of Asmat had no title and possession and sold the said land to the defendant No. 15 who in collusion with the defendant Nos. 1-12 threatened to dispossess the plaintiff from the suit land on 25-3-84 which led the plaintiff to launch the suit. 

 3. The suit was resisted by the defendant No. 15 on the ground, inter alia, that the suit is barred under section 66 of the Code of Civil Procedure and then the defendant averred that the land measuring 4.41 acres comprising CS Khatian No. 689 belonged to Rashid Howlader and Menhajuddin Howlader. The superior landlord Laha Babu and others for realisation of rent instituted rent suit in the year 1930 and in execution of rent decree No. 860/31 auction sold the land of CS Khatian No. 687 and Asmat Ali Howlader auction purchased the land with his own money and got possession in the land. While Asmat Ali had been proceeding to annul the encumbrance as regards under tenancy of Khatian Nos. 688 and 689 there had been an amicable arrangement by which the original tenant Safaruddin made over 0.62 decimals of land of plot No. 1822 and 0.30 decimals from plot No. 1824/2134 comprising Khatian No. 688 in favour of Asmat Ali and in respect of land with an area of 3.49 acre of the said Khatian to the three sons of Safaruddin remained as sub-tenants under Asmat Ali and RS Khatian was prepared accordingly. Thus Asmat Ali by auction purchase acquired 2.71 acres of land of Khatian No. 689 and 0.92 decimals of Khatian No. 688 and owned and possessed 3.63 acres which is the suit land. After the death of Asmat Ali the defendant Nos. 1-14 being his heirs got the suit land. Further case of the defendant is, that the defendant Nos. 1-6 and 9-12 entered into agreements for sale with the defendant No. 15 by two registered sale deeds dated 7-9-83 and the defendant has been in possession and enjoying the land on payment of rent. 

 5. Mr. Sk Razzaque Ali the learned Advocate, has appeared in support of the Rule and he has in the first place contended that the learned Appellate Court failed to consider the documentary evidence adduced by the plaintiff in coming to a conclusion with regard to the real controversy between the parties in the suit. He has pointed out particularly from Exhibit 7, the kabala dated 28-3-1923 showing transfer of 0.92 decimals of land by Safaruddin Faraji to the father of the plaintiff and Exhibit 6(a) which indicates that Menhajuddin had been in possession of that portion of the land as purchaser and he had the under raiyati right which was inherited by him. He further contended that the document No. 6(a) having presumption of correctness has not been evaluated and the rent receipts Exhibit 3 series have not been considered along with the oral testimony in arriving at a finding of possession of plaintiff in the suit land and, consequently, there has been total misreading and non-consideration of the material evidence occasioning failure of justice. The 2nd branch of submission of Mr.Sk Razzaque Ali is that Kha schedule land which is the suit land comprises CS Khatian Nos. 688 and 689 constituted under- tenancy under CS Khatian No. 687 and there having no khas land, the auction purchaser Asmat Ali could not have acquired any title and interest in the land of Khatian Nos. 688 and 689 unless the under tenancy is annulled by service of notice as contemplated under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act and he says that there is no proof of annulment of under tenancies and the tenant having Kolkarsha or Dar karsha right continued to be the tenant in the holdings and the plaintiff got title not on the basis of auction purchase but by way of inheritance and purchase from the original tenants. The courts below having not considered this aspect of the case committed error of law occasioning failure of justice and in this regard reliance has been made on different cases of Indian jurisdiction. First case is the case of Nibaran Chandra Ghosh and others vs Pratap Chandra Chowdhury and others reported in 44 CWN 141. In that case it has been held: 

 "A sub-lease not valid against the sub-lessor's landlord under section 85 of the Bengal Tenancy Act (now repealed) is nevertheless valid against the sub-lessor as also against a third party who purchases the sub-lessor's interest at a certificate sale and transferees from him". 

 7. In the above cited case in a suit for declaration of title and ejectment of the under raiyat brought by transferee from certificate purchaser the question was raised that an under raiyati created by sub-lease by a raiyat is thus an encumbrance against a transferee from the certificate purchaser of the raiyat and must be duly annulled before the under raiyat can be ejected. In the facts of the case prayer for ejectment was refused for not having annulled the encumbrances by notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Next case that has been referred to is AIR 1937 (All) 176, Biahan Dayal vs Kesho Prasad and another, In that case section 66 of the Code of Civil Procedure came under consideration and it was held that where a person purchases some property at an auction sale solely for himself and if another person claims that the purchases in fact was made by the auction jointly on his behalf (auction purchaser's) and the claimant's predecessor such claim is barred under section 66,Code of Civil Procedure. The substantial thing to be considered is that auction purchaser who is resisting the claim, claims title to the property under a purchase certified by the court, and if the property in dispute is part of the property so purchased auction purchaser is protected. A distinction should not be drawn between the cases where the whole of the property purchased is claimed and where the claimant says that he purchased only a share in the property mentioned in the sale certificate In other case the auction purchaser claims title under a purchase certified by the court and the claim comes within the mischief of section 66 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Following the pronouncement of their Lordships of the Privy Council it was further held that the primary object of the section seems to be that the certified purchase should be deemed to be conclusive arid no one should be allowed to challenge it, unless he comes within the exceptions mentioned in the section itself. The next case referred to is AIR 1937 (Patna) 324 Naji Rajob Ali vs SkAktar Ali. In that case the applicability of section 66 of the Code of Civil Procedure was considered in deciding a case under Chotanagpur Tenancy Act (VI of 1908) and under the Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act clause I of section 265 provided that Chotanagpur Tenancy Act by implication renders the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure inapplicable to matters before the Deputy Commissioners except insofar as, the provision of the Code are applied to such matters by rule. 

 Both the Courts below held that the plaintiffs, are not entitled to claim enhanced rent from the defendants for the Osat Taluk, but have allowed a decree to the plaintiffs, in respect of arrears of rent at the old rate of rent. The plaintiffs appealed and two points were raised on their behalf. In the first place it was argued that the Mukarari Osat Taluks created by. Basanta are not binding upon the plaintiffs inasmuch as Basanta who was a non Mukarari tenure holder could not create a Mukarari under tenure or, in other words, he could not confer upon his tenants a higher right than what he himself possessed. Courts below relied upon section 179 of the Bengal Tenancy Act in support of their view that a permanent tenure holder is entitled to create a Mukarari under tenure which will be binding upon the purchaser of the tenure unless annulled under section 167 of the Act. The view taken by the courts below was upheld. That was a case for enhancement of rent. The case before me is to be decided in the context of the plaintiffs claim as founded in the plaint. It is evident from the plaint case that after the sudden purchase the plaintiff did not get possession in the land as the under tenancy which is an encumbrance against the certified encumbrances against the certified purchaser had not been annulled and further asserted that during the plaintiffs minority the said maternal uncle Asmat Ali managed the auction purchased land and rent was paid in the name of Asmat Ali. It is also admitted in the plaint that during the SA and RS settlement operation the name of Asmat Ali was recorded as per advice of the plaintiff. 

 9. Admittedly the auction sale took place in 1931 after the CS record was prepared and the purchase was made by the plaintiff in the name of Asmat Ali Howlader. Be it noted that the plaintiff has not made out any case in the plaint that even after the auction purchase in the name of Asmat Ali whom he designates as benamder, the predecessor of the plaintiff being in possession of the land for a long period exceeding 12 years or by custom had acquired the occupancy right in the land sold in rent decree which he inherited independent of the benami purchase and that right having not been annulled under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act the plaintiff became the tenant under certificate purchase and continued to remain so on payment of rent and that subsequently the plaintiff became tenant under the Government after the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into being. It is the admitted case of the plaintiff that the purchase in the court was made in the benami of Asmat Ali, rent was paid although in the name of Asmat Ali and the principal plaintiff has averred in the plaint that he being the real purchaser had not annulled the encumbrances and in the SA operation the record of right was prepared in the name of Asmat Ali under his advice, such being the position the cases cited would be of no assistance to the plaintiff. Rather the principle laid down in Bishan Dayal vs Kesho Prasad and another reported in AIR 1937 (All) 176 would support the plea of the defendant.

2. Plaintiff-respondents filed a suit being Other Class Suit No. 1 of 1966 against the Government in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Mymensingh for declaration of their title to the suit land and that their possession was not unauthorised and that the entry of the name of Government in record of rights was wrong. On behalf of the Government it was contended that the suit land vested in the Government as a result of Government Gazette Notification No. 1524 dated 21st December 1957 and that the forest department is in possession of the suit land. Further, the documents of plaintiff-respondents are fraudulent, they having no right, title and interest in the suit land. 

 6. Mr. M.H. Khondker, Counsel for the plaintiff-respondents, submitted that the plaintiffs purchased some lands of plot No.58 from different persons who took pattan from Deldoar Estate and the rest of the land of the said plot was taken settlement of by them on payment of rent. Plaintiffs also purchased out of plot Nos.626, 646 and 651 from different persons who had taken paten of these plots. Plaintiffs are in possession of these plots for more than 30 years and have also got their dwelling house in plot No. 58. These lands were wrongly recorded in the name of the Government in the recent record of rights. The learned Counsel submitted that as the suit had been disposed of long before the passing of Ordinance No. XXXIII of 1982 the suit cannot be said to have retrospectively abated. In support of the judgment of the High Court Division the learned Counsel submitted that the suit having been disposed of long ago and therefore, being not pending the principle that appeal is the continuation of the suit is not attracted in the present case for directing abatement of the suit by virtue of the aforesaid provisions of the Ordinance.

2. Circumstances giving rise to this air peal may be described as follows: Respondent as plaintiff filed O.C. Suit No. 225 of 1960 in the Court of Munsif, Rajshahi, for recovery of khas possession of the suit land by ejecting the appellant defendant. He claimed the appellant to be his tenant from month to month in respect of the suit premises. The appellant denied the landlord-tenant relationship with the respondent and set up a claim of his independent title on the basis of purchase. The suit land consists of 3 Plots. Nos. 25, 26 and 27 recorded under three separate C.S. Khatians, Plot No. 24 belonged to Kalicharan; plot No. 27 belonged to Shashi Bhushan and Plot No. 25 belonged to Swarna Baishnabi. According to the respondent, Kali Charan purchased the other two plots, got his name mutated in the landlord's sherista, paid rent for those plots till his death, and after him his son, Pati Ram, defendant No. 2, inherited the property and possessed it in the same way. Defendant No. 2 executed a Power of Attorney dated 2-1-51. Ext. 1, in favour of one Sekandar giving him full power to transfer the suit land and Sekandar accordingly transferred the suit land consisting of all the three plots to the plaintiff by executing a registered sale-deed dated 9-4-51, Ext. 2. Plaintiff immediately took possession, constructed a few huts on the land and inducted thereon defendant No. 1 as a monthly tenant at a rental of Tk. 10/- from Chaitra 1358 B.S. The defendant after paying rent for a few months started defaulting and during "Rent-roll Operation" unsuccessfully tried to get his name recorded in the khatian as owner of the suit premises. The Revenue authorities after rejections recorded the plaintiff's name in the S.A. Khatian. Thereafter defendant No. 1 procured a sale-deed from Golap Sundari, Shashi, Bhusan's wife, and therewith tried to assert his title. The plaintiff served a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act upon defendant No. 1 and thereby terminating the tenancy, filed the suit for ejectment. Contention of defendant No.1 was that he was never a tenant of the plaintiff, but that he had first entered into plot. No. 27 with permission of Golap Sundari in 1949 erected the huts thereon and entered into an agreement with her for sale of this plot on 26-11-56 and thereafter, by a registered sale-deed dated 3-8-59 purchased the plot. As to plot No. 26 which was inherited by Pati Ram from Kali Charan, defendant No. 1 claimed that by an agreement with Pati Ram, for sale he got possession of this plot from 1949, but Pati Ram subsequently proved faithless, sided with the plaintiff, and disowned the agreement. As to plot No. 25, his claim is that as it was lying vacant he took over its possession. He denied the plaintiff's title to the suit premises and particularly denied that he was inducted by plaintiff as a monthly tenant. 

 5. Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed learned Advocate for the respondent, on the other hand has contended that the question involved in this appeal is not purely a question of fact, but it involves a substantial question-of law in that some important documents on the basis of which the respondent claims title have been misconstrued by the lower Appellate Court The learned Advocate has pointed out that though in a suit for ejectment the question of title is not directly an issue still in this case this question was incidentally gone into, and rightly so, but while considering the question of title the lower Appellate Court illegally and on erroneous view of law rejected the plaintiff's sale-deed, Ext. 2 based on the Power of Attorney, Ext. 1. The learned Counsel has further contended that a great number of Rent-receipts, Ext. 3 series, showing payment of rent by Kalicharan and thereafter, by his son, Pati Ram, both before and after the State Acquisition, and the record of rights, namely, S.A. Khatian in favour of the respondent, have been brushed aside by the learned District Judge on erroneous view of law and as such though the question involved, whether the landlord tenant relationship exists between the parties is a question of fact, yet the proper legal effect of the proved fact is essentially a question of law ; at best, the question involved in this case is a mixed question of law and fact. In deciding the question of fact, it has been further argued, the learned District Judge misdirected himself and as such his finding is not immune from interference in second appeal. 

 7. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed learned Counsel contends that the question to be decided in this case is a question of fact and this does not involve an issue of law merely because some documents have been interpreted and construed. He has made a distinction between constructions of a document which is an instrument of title or is otherwise direct foundation of rights, and construction of a document which is not a document of title but is a document containing items of evidence or historical narration. On this point he seeks support from an observation of the Judicial Committee of Privy Council in the case of Midnapur Zimindary Company Vs. Uma Charan, AIR 1923 PC, 187. In that case, the date of an under-tenure was to be traced out and fixed from contents of some documents and oral evidence. No document creating the under-tenure came up for consideration, but some documents giving the historical narration of the under-tenure were construed and thereupon the High Court reversed the finding of fact arrived at by the lower Appellate Court. The Privy Council while reversing the High Court's judgment and restoring that of the lower appellate court observed: 

 "Where the question to be decided is one of fact, it does not involve an issue of law merely because documents, which were not instruments of title or contracts or statutes or otherwise the direct foundation of rights but were really historical materials have to be construed for the purpose.............There is no ground for a second appeal upon a question of fact unless it can be shown that the lower Appellate Court misdirected itself in point of law in dealing with this question upon the evidence." 

 8. The sale-deed, Ext. 2 includes three plots two of which namely Nos. 25 and 27 did not originally belong to Kalicharan; but evidence led by the plaintiff is that Kalicharan purchased those two plots, got his name mutated in the Landlord's sherista and paid rent accordingly. In support of this claim rent-receipt Ext. 3 to 3(h) have been produced. The learned District Judge, however, excluded these rent-receipts from consideration taking the view that the rent-receipts though purportedly issued by the ex-landlord, do not relate to the suit plots. The High Court Division disagreed with this view and observed, we think rightly, that unless a tenant's name is recorded in the Rent-Roll by mutation he cannot pay rent. The High Court Division further found that although the plot numbers were not mentioned in the receipts, other particulars including the exact amount of rent were specifically mentioned there and that this fact established connection between them and the plots in question. On the other hand, no rent was paid by Shashi Bhusan or his wife Golap Sundari or Swarna Baishnabi (owner of plot No. 25) at any time before the State Acquisition. Thereafter rent for all the three plots was paid to the government by Pati Ram defendant No. 2, son of Kalicharan, as per rent-receipts Exts.3(h)to 3 (p): and since plaintiff's purchase in 1951 he has been paying the rent The rent-receipts were excluded from consideration by the lower Appellate Court taking the view that these are provisional receipts and that they carry little weight in that “any person interested in a land may pay rent to the Government Acquired Estate". This view is erroneous for rent-receipts, though not documents of title are important items of evidence of possession and may be used as collateral evidence of title since possession generally follows title. Again, plaintiff's name has also been recorded in the S.A. Khatian prepared in the period immediately following the whole-sale state-acquisition in 1956 and all objections raised by defendant No. 1 were overruled by the Revenue-officer and then by the appellate authority. 

 But in a subsequent case, Dhanna Mal v Roy Bahadur Moti Sagar, AIR J972 PC 102, the Privy Council held that whether a tenancy is permanent is a question of law and observed the question whether a tenancy is permanent or precarious is one of .legal inference from fact and not itself a question of fact". It arose from a suit for recovery of rent and ejectment. Rent at enhanced rate was demanded by the landlord, but enhancement of rent was not permissible if the tenancy was permanent. The tenant did not plead in his written statement that the tenancy was permanent, and in a previous suit for rent he had submitted to the enhancement of rent. The lower Appellate Court found in favour of the tenant that the tenancy was permanent, but the High Court in second appeal reversed the finding and held the tenancy to be temporary taking the view that the question involved is an issue of law. High Court's decision was upheld "by the Privy Council which also approved of the High Court's describing the question as "a mixed question of law and fact", with warning that "insofar as dependsupon fact, the finding of the first appellate court must be accepted". In the case of Walt Mohammad v. Mohammad Baks, AIR 1930 PC. 91 the Privy Council reversed the decision of the High Court which had interfered, in second appeal, with the .lower Appellate Court's decision regarding a question of fact which was whether the land under a mortgage was sold away by the mortgagee. The Privy Council rejected the contention that "entries in the record-of-rights were foundations of title" but held them to be mere items of evidence to be produced by the vendee to prove the sale. 

 14. I n the well- known case of Sm. Bivabati Vs. Ramendra Narayan, AIR 1947 PC 20, the Privy Council reiterated "the established practice of the Board to decline to review the evidence for the third time where there are concurrent judgments of two courts on a pure question of fact" particularly when the circumstances justifying departure from the practice are not made out. One of those circumstance as set out in that judgment is "some miscarriage of justice or violation of some principle of law or practice...............violation being such a proposition of law that" if it is corrected the finding cannot stand". In every case the general principle to be followed is that a finding of face arrived at by the court of first appeal shall not be disturbed by the High Court, but a finding of fact to attain immunity from attack in second appeal must be based on evidence. If a finding is not based on evidence or if it is based on utter inadequacy of evidence on which no reasonable conclusion can be reached, then interference therewith in second appeal is certainly justified. Misreading of evidence is a ground for interference but mis-appreciation of evidence is not. A finding which is inconsistent with the evidence on record must call for interference in second, appeal. Again, if a decision of the lower Appellate Court consists of both 'oral and documentary evidence but a part of the documentary evidence is misunderstood it will not provide a ground for interference when the document does not form the preponderance of the evidence. High Court's power in second appeal does not include power to review the evidence to come to a finding of its own on a question of fact, but the High Court can give a finding which has not been given by the lower appellate court on the evidence on record; interference on that ground will be quite lawful. After all, every case must be decided on the facts and circumstances of that case keeping in view these broad principles.

full_judgment:
2. Relevant facts necessary for disposal of the aforesaid petitions are that the writ petitioner Md Wais Hossain being aggrieved by the order of the Revenue Officer in Objection Case No 1634 filed an appeal under rule 31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 being Appeal No. 108449 of 2007, the appeal was heard by Zonal Settlement Officer, Jessore Zone, Jessore and the Appeal Officer (hereinafter referred to as the Zonal Settlement Officer) and the Zonal Settlement Officer upon hearing both the parties by order No. 4 dated 19-12-2007 allowed the said appeal; after passing the aforesaid order in Appeal No. 108449 of 2007, Jahanara Khatun and others filed Miscellaneous Case No. 139 of 2013; thereafter, the Sadar Assistant Settlement Officer, Jessore Zone, Jessore (shortly, Sadar Assistant Settlement Officer) issued a notice vide Memo No. জোসেঅ/যশো/৬/৩২/খন্ড-৬/এস-১১১০ dated 31-3-2013 (the impugned notice) to the writ petitioner for appearing before the Zonal Settlement Officer i.e. the Appeal Officer; earlier a three members committee was formed for giving opinion in respect of re-hearing of the appeal and the said committee upon thorough examination and consideration of the materials on record, on 18-11-2012 opined that there was/is no scope of re-hearing of the appeal but it was not considered by the Zonal Settlement Officer. Whereupon, the writ petitioner respondent preferred Writ Petition No. 3697 of 2013 and obtained a Rule. 

 5. After the death of the said Ajimunnesa, Ali Insan, father of the writ petitioner, had tried to grab the entire disputed land owned by his mother late Ajimunnesa and recorded the disputed land solely in his name by exercising fraud. Hence, Jahanara Khatun (daughter of late Ajimunnesa) through her son Masud Hossain and Ahsanullah, another son of Ali Hasan filed cases before the Zonal Settlement Officer, Jessore following which notices were issued by the Sadar Assistant Settlement Officer, Zonal Settlement Office, Jessore Zone, Jessore for appearing to present their cases. These cases were subsequently numbered as Appeal Case Nos. 109316 of 2008, 109317 of 2008, 140202 of 2010 and 108449 of 2007. Eventually, writ petitioner's appeal was allowed and that of Rowshan Ara Khatun, Jahan Ara Khatun etc. were rejected. 

 9. Mr Momtazuddin Fakir, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr Nurul Islam Bhuiyan, Advocate-on-record for the petitioner in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2605 of 2017 takes us through the impugned Judgment and order dated 3-4-2017 passed by the High Court Division as well as the materials on record and submits that the High Court Division passed the Judgment and order on surmises and conjectures. He next submits that the High Court Division failed to appreciate that the three members committee was formed for giving opinion in respect of re-hearing of the appeal on examination and consideration of records and to identify if the documents used by the writ petitioner is forged and the said committee gave a wrong opinion to the effect that there was no scope of rehearing of the appeal. 

 11. Mr Soumendra Nath Biswas, the learned Deputy Attorney-General instructed by Mr Haridas Paul, advocate-on-record appearing for the petitioners in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2883 of 2017 adopted the arguments as advanced by Mr Md Momtazuddin Fakir. 

 12. Mr Khurshid Alam Khan, the learned Senior Advocate instructed by Mr, Md, Zahirul Islam, the learned Advocate-on-record appearing for the respondents in both the cases supports the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and submits that there is no element of fraud and, as such, there is no scope for review/re-hearing of the rule 42A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955. 

 14. We have examined the writ petition, the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division and the connected materials on record. 

 15. We have also examined the relevant provision of Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 which reads as under: "42A. Correction of fraudulent entry before final publication of record-of-rights —The Revenue-officer, with the additional designation of 'Settlement Officer' shall, on receipt of an application or on receipt of an official report for the correction of an entry that has been procured by fraud in record-of-rights before final publication thereof, after consulting relevant records and making such other enquiries as he deems necessary, direct excision of the fraudulent entry and his act in doing so shall not be open to appeal. At the same time, the Revenue-officer shall make the correct entry after giving the parties concerned a hearing and recording his finding in a formal proceeding for the purpose of future reference." 

 18. Similarly in Aftab Ali Sheikh vs Director, Land Records, reported in 58 DLR 397 wherein it has been held that: "Under Rule 44 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955, the Director of Land Records and Surveys has been vested with the power to discharge all the functions of a Revenue Officer under the said chapter and shall have all the powers of a Settlement Officer under Rule 42A along with some other Rules in respect of all operations under Chapter XVII of the SAT Act but unless there is a case of fraud or having procured the appellate judgment in making the entry by fraud Rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 has no manner of application." 

 19. In this decision also it has been clearly stated that in case of making entry by practicing fraud Rule 44A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 has no manner of application. In the instant case respondent No. 7 as well as the Government clearly stated that fraud has committed by Md Wais Hossain in obtaining entry in the record by practicing fraud. 

 22. Thus, it appears that the respondent Md Wais Mia got the land recorded for the disputed land admittedly excepting the other heirs of Azimunnessa through a registered deed which is a fraudulent deed with reasons thereof.

 4. IN this way by 8 registered sale deeds plaintiffs became owner and possessor of three Katha nine chataks of land with structures standing thereon to the knowledge of all including the defendants.  7. Defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement and in the written statement the plaint case was denied line by line and it is his specific case that predecessor of the plaintiffs purchased land from Sree Sarnalata Dey when Title Suit No. 141 of 1945 was pending and this purchase is hit by lis pendency, Plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 171 of 1985 impleading Kaniz Fatema, predecessor of the defendant No. 1 Suit was dismissed. Plaintiffs filed Title Appeal No. 120 of 1957 and thereafter plaintiffs filed Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 195 of 1958 and these appeals were dismissed thereby title of Sarnalata, predecessor of the plaintiffs and also of the plaintiffs totally lost and extinguished. It is further case of this defendant that suit land originally belongs to Maharaj of Durgapur, Mymensingh and CS Khatian was prepared in the name of heirs of Maharaj Durgapur, Mymensingh who filed Partition Suit No. 145 of 1927 in the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, 4th Court, Mymensingh and in that suit, sham for an area of 1475 Ajutangsha was allowed to Raja Shibkrishna Sing. For the remaining land of the aforesaid dag the other heirs who got saham, from them, Charulata Paul by registered deed No. 2369 dated 19-9-1938 purchased 4 kathas and 1 chha tak 6½ gandas of land and got possession and from Charulata Paul, Kaniz Fatema by registered deed No. 4113 in 1950 purchased the said land ands got possession. Direndra Chandra Sing and other 3 sons of raja Shibkrishna Sing also got 4/7 shares and for title and recovery of possession against Charulata Paul, Sarnalata Paul and others as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 141 of 1945 in the court of Sub-ordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka renumbered before the court of additional Sub-ordinate Judge, Dhaka as Title Suit No. 40 of 1951. The suit was dismissed on 25-5-1951 and while the said suit was pending Sarnalata Paul sold some land to Syed Ali Habib. Sarnalata Dey did not get any land in the suit and by purchase from Sarnalata Dey, Syed Ali Habib also did not get any land as his purchase was hit by lis pendency. Kaniz Fatema, the predecessor of defendant purchased the decree of that suit on 22-4-1952 and replaced his name as decree holder and by executing decree through Title Execution case No. 66 of 1952 of Court of 5th Sub-ordinate Judge, Dhaka wherein Advocate Commissioners were appointed, got 0488 Ajutangsha of land and got possession by court on 25/8/1953 and demarcated by opening khatian No. 16842/13. The heirs of Syed Ai Habib filed Title Suit No. 171 of 1955 before the Munsif, 6th Court, Dhaka for declaration of title and for khash possession against the mother of this defendant, Kaniz Fatema as defendant. The suit was dismissed on 28-6-1957, against which Title Appeal No. 120 of 1957 was filed. Appeal was dismissed on 5-11-1957. Against which decision plaintiffs of that suit filed Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 195 of 1958 before the High Court Division. This appeal also dismissed by the High Court Division by judgment dated 25-8-1959. Against that decision, plaintiffs of that suit did not take any step as such, plaintiffs have no title over the suit property as they purchased the land from a person who had no title and possession over the suit land. In this way Kaniz Fatema by purchase became owner of 4 khathas 1 Chhatak = .0608 Ajutangsha of land and by decree got .1158 Ajutangsha of land. Later on, Kaniz Fatema sold .856 Ajutangsha of land to Lutfar Rahman and retain. 0302 Ajutangsha of land was is in her possession till her death. In the recent survey, the name of Kaniz Fatema was first recorded for 1022 Ajutangsha of land, later on, by deducting 0.056, Ajutangsha of land which was sold and recorded in the name of Lutfor Rahman, 0240 Ajutangsha of land was recorded in the name of Kaniz Fatema in khatian No. 5523 and 5520. It is further case of this defendant that in schedule dag of Kaniz Fatema, plaintiffs surreptitiously in Mutation Case No. 2177/1994-95 mutated their names of which defendant after came to know filed Miscellaneous Case No. 20/1997-98 which was allowed and recording of the name of the plaintiffs in Mutation Case No. 2177/1994-95 was cancelled on contested hearing. Against the decision of Miscellaneous Case No. 20/1997-98, Miscellaneous Appeal No. 112 of 2005 was filed before the Assistant Commis-sioner (Revenue), Dhaka which was also dismissed.  13. On the submissions of the learned Advocates and materials on record two questions calls for determinations, i) whether plaintiffs' acquired title in the suit property by purchase from Majid and ii) whether the suit on the cause of action as given by the plaintiffs is maintainable. 

 17. In the question mutation. It appears in Mutation Case No. 2177/1994-95 mutation was done in faovur of plaintiffs but when defendant No. 1 came to know of such wrong recording, he filed Miscellaneous Case No. 20/1994-98 and got the mutation in favour of plaintiffs set-aside. It appears from Exhibit 'Uma' khatian No. 870/1 the suit land recorded in the name of defendant and from Exhibit `Cha' enquiry report shows that the defendants are in possession. From Exhibit `Cha' Fazlur Rahman plaintiff claimed he got mutation of .0473 Ajutangsha of land but he has found in possession of 0.0006 Ajutangsha of land. From Exhibit `Chha' it appears that plaintiffs appeal being time barred was rejected and also Assistant Commissioner found that mutation in favour of plaintiff was done contradictory to the decision of the High Court Division passed in Second Appeal No. 195 of 1998. Exhibit 'Ja' is decision of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) dismissing Miscellaneous Appeal No. 18 of 2005 filed by the plaintiff. Exhibit 'Ja-1' is Miscellaneous Appeal No. 18 of 2005 filed by the plaintiff and exhibt 'Jha' is the power of attorney. 

 "144 B Bar to Jurisdiction of Civil Court-(1) When an order has been made under sub-section 1 of section 144 directing the preparation of revision of record of rights in respect of any area, then, subject to the provisions of section 111, a civil Court shall not entertain any suit or application for the alternation of any rent or determination of the status of any tenant of the incidents of any tenancy in such area and if any such suit or application relating to such area is pending before a civil Court on or after the date of such order, it shall not be further proceeded with and shall abate and if any judgment, decree or order has been passed in any such suit for any order has been passed on any such application, after the said date, it shall be inoperative and of no legal effect. 

 (2) No suit or application shall be brought in a civil Court in respect of any order directing the preparation or revision of record-of-rights under this Chapter or in respect of framing, publication, signing or attesting of such a record or any part of it, and if any such suit or application is pending before a civil Court, it shall not be further proceeded with and shall abate and if any judgment, decree or order has been passed in any such suit or any order has been passed on any such application, it shall be inoperative and of no legal effect."

full_judgment:
4. The facts of the case relevant for disposal of the Rule, in brief, are that the petitioners in all the four writ petitions are lessees of property of Ain Uddin Haider and Faizunnessa Waqf Estate for 99 years. Their claim is that they have been in lawful possession of the  property) since the  grant of their respective leases and that during the latest land survey the property in question was recorded in the name of the Waqf Estate. It is further stated in the petition that a Title Suit being No. 809 of 2008 was filed for declaration of title, which is pending in the Court of Additional District Judge, Dhaka. It is admitted in the petition that' after the eviction notice dated 7-2-2008 the structures and buildings standing on the petitioner's land were demolished during the eviction drive on 13-2-2008, which was reported in the Daily Samokal on 15-2-2008 (Annexure-P). 

 10. The learned Advocate for the petitioner next submits that the petitioners land forms part of the Ain Uddin Haider and Faizunnessa Waqf Estate and it was published in the record of rights on 27-7- 2005. He submits that the Khatian notification dated 31-7-2005 showing Ain Uddin Haider and Faizunnessa Waqf Estate to be the owners of the property carries with it a presumption of correctness of the record under section 144(7) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. He submits that such notification by the Government as published in the record of rights overrides any earlier notification under section 5(7) of the 1'948 Act. He submits that it is a legal presumption that the government must know about its earlier notification and, therefore, the effect of the later notification is to strike out the earlier one. He submits that the order of eviction is an affront to the pending judicial proceeding and it is an attempt to pre-empt the judgment in the title suit pending before the competent Civil Court. 

 14. During the course of hearing we requested the learned Deputy Attorney-General to make available the records of LA Case No. 90/65-66 and 5/72- 73 for our perusal. We found that the Order/ Note Sheets of the LA Case No. 90/65-66 are within the records. But those of LA Case No. 5/72-73 are found to be post -1991. However, the notices are found in the correspondence portion of the file, produced before us, including copies of the notices issued. After our own perusal, we allowed the learned Advocates for the petitioners to peruse the records of the LA cases. 

 17. We find from the records of LA Case No. 5/72-73 that notice under section 3 was issued to the Ms Eastern Housing Limited as the owner and occupier to hand over possession of the land by 10- 11-72 for Expanded Urban Housing at Mirpur. The area of land mentioned was 654.9851 acres. We find from this file that, land was made over to the requiring body on 8-4-74 from out of the land requisitioned for Eastern Housing, the new requiring body being গৃহ নির্মান ও পুনবার্সন. 

 19. We find from the records that in LA No. 5/72-73 notices under section 3 were issued and land was handed over to the requiring body from the possession of Eastern Housing, the notice under section 5(1) was issued on 1-4-74. The requiring body is mentioned as Expanded Urban Housing at Mirpur under the Department named গৃহ নির্মান ও পুনবার্সন. We also find a certificate of delivery of possession of land measuring 608.641 acres taken over by the Sub-Divisional Engineer, Greeha Nirman-o- Punarbasan, Mirpur. 

 23. The decision of the High Court Division was challenged in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 68 of 2004, wherein the judgment and order of the High Court Division was upheld dismissing the Petition for Leave to Appeal, which had been filed by one Abdullah Al Mamun, who we find is the Secretary of the Management Committee of the Waqf Estate. We also note that there were some other writ petitions, namely WP No. 7763 of 2005, 7217 of 2002, 2724 of 1999 and 4247 of 2002, wherein the same acquisition Notification dated 15-10-74 was challenged. These Rules were also discharged by the High Court Division and the Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal were filed before the. Appellate Division in Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal Nos. 1152, 1219 and 1660 of 2007. The leave petitions were rejected by the Appellate Division as barred by limitation and also on merit relying upon the fact that the matter had already been decided by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 68 of 2004 on merit. We note from the materials on record that Writ Petitions Nos. 2415, 3349, 3484, 3353, 3480, 3345, 3347, 3346, and 3478 of 1999 were instituted challenging the legality of LA Case No. 5/72-73 and were all discharged with the observation that all the requirements of sections 3, 4 and 5 of the 1948 Act have been duly complied in acquiring the land in LA Case No. 5/72-73 and finding that, therefore, the acquisition-Notification issued under section 5(7) was not issued without lawful authority.

3. The plaint case, in short, is that, 8 annas of plot No. 1522 measuring 0.08 acre, and 0.31 acre of plot No. 1524 appertaining to RS Khatian No. 2325 and SA Khatian No. 992 originally belonged to Kashem Ali and Sorju Bala. Other 8 annas of plot No. 1522 was owned and possessed by the plaintiff and SA Khatian Nos. 1446 and 1333 were recorded in his name. The suit land measuring 0.39 acre was purchased by Kali Mohan Mukhopadhya on an auction sale held on 5-1-1953. Said Kali Mohan Mukhopadhya obtained sale certificate and got possession of the land through court on 18-4-1954. 

 6. Defendant Nos.1 and 2, Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) Bakhergonj and Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Barisal were the original defendants and defendants 3, 4, 5 and 6 were subsequently added. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 though filed a written statement but ultimately did not contest the suit. The courts below therefore, did not record their case as stated by them in their written statement in the judgment. Defendant No.3 having died his heirs defendant Nos. 3(Ka) to 3(Chha) and defendant No.4 jointly filed a written statement and contested the suit. Similarly, defendant Nos. 5 and 6 also contested the suit by filing another written statement. 

 12. Mr Abdus Sobhan Tarafder, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, drew my attention to the fact that in the appeal, the petitioners made an application for amendment of the plaint on the ground that aforesaid PW 1 did not make such a statement that his father did not possess the suit land by virtue of purchase or that defendant No. 3 possessed the suit land. PW 1 actually deposed that they possessed the suit land by virtue of purchase and the defendant No.3 did not possess the suit land. In the first sentence 'No' was added and in the last sentence 'No' was omitted due to mistake. They, therefore, prayed for adding further relief for confirmation of possession in the suit land as consequential to the main prayer for declaration of title on payment of ad-valorem court fee. Without applying its mind the appellate Court rejected the said application as irrelevant and belated. Mr Abdus Sobhan Tarafder also submitted that in the trial Court, the plaintiff proved their title and possession but the trial Court without considering the evidence on record disposed of the suit on those mistaken statements as recorded. Appellate Court also without properly framing the points for determination and discussing the evidence on record disposed of the appeal by a non- speaking judgment in confirming the judgment of the trial Court and the judgment of the appellate Court is no judgment in the eye of law, particularly, under Order 41 rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 16. I have perused the judgments of the courts below and the revision application upon which the above Rule was issued. I have also examined the evidence, both oral and documentary, on record. 

 17. The case of the plaintiffs-petitioners is that, Kashem Ali and Sarujo Bala were the original owners in possession of the suit lands. Then, Kali Mohan Mukherjee purchased the suit lands in an auction held on 6-1-1953. He obtained a sale certificate and got physical possession of the lands on 18-4-1954. He also annulled all encumbrances. While Kali Mohan was thus in possession, he transferred the suit lands by a registered deed of sale dated  8-6-1962 to Afsar Ali Howlader and Mokter Ali Howlader. These two brothers, Howladers possessed for some time and then, sold the suit lands to Tayeb Ali, father of the present plaintiffs, by registered sale deed dated 10-4-1967. Tayeb Ali possessed the suit lands for more than the statutory period of 1iyears and then died leaving the present plaintiffs as his only heirs and legal representatives. During the survey under the state acquisitions, the record of rights in respect of the suit lands were wrongly prepared in the names of said original owners, Kashem Ali and Sarujo Bala who were divested of all their interest in the suit lands after the auction sale, and such record had no basis but cast a doubt on the title of the petitioners. 

 20. The trial Court also found the notice Exhibit No. 2 by which Kali Mohan annulled all the encumbrances and his employees collected rents from the 'Karsha' raiyots. But the court was of the view that the right or interest of the 'Karsha' raiyots was not disappeared. No proceeding was instituted for eviction of the 'Karsha' raiyots. The SA record of rights was prepared in the names of Kashem Ali and Sarujo Bala to the extent of 12 annas and 4 ann as respectively. This finding of the trial Court is however contrary to the case of both defendants 3 and 4 and also of defendants 5 and 6. Their common case is that, during the partition in 1947, both Kashem Ali and Sarujo Bala migrated to India and settled there. Kashem Ali died there. In view of its own findings on title as stated above, the finding of the court that Kali Mohan Mukherjee possessed the suit lands was not proved is not only incongruous but also contrary to the pleadings as well as the evidence on record. 

 21. The trial Court also found that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 264 of 1984, declared the initiation of a VP Case in respect of the suit lands illegal, and without any lawful jurisdiction, (Exhibit No. 'Uma' and 'Uma-1 '). Appeal preferred by a brother of defendants 5 and 6 therefrom being Title Appeal No. 103 of 1989 was also dismissed. The vested property authority did not take any step against the decree and, as such, the said authority cannot have now anything to say. The trial Court therefore concluded that defendants 5 and 6 could not have any right or interest as lessee under the vested properties authority. It also held that defendant Nos. 5 and 6 failed to prove that they are the heirs of the original recorded tenant, Kashem Ali, Exhibit No. 'Nia'. 

 24. It is my misfortune that I had to consider the judgment of the trial Court elaborately because I could not find any consideration by the appellate Court of the cases of the parties. The appellate Court below just recorded its concurrence with the findings of the trial Court on the issues as framed in the suit, and held that it did not find any reason to differ with the decision of the trial Court on main issues that the plaintiffs could not get any relief and the suit would be dismissed. Before recording its conformance, it did not consider a single document adduced by the parties nor the testimony of any witness. I find the disposal of the appeal did not receive any application of mind of the Subordinate Judge, Third Court, Barisal who heard the appeal. Similarly, he failed to consider the application for amendment of the plaint made on 3-5-1995. 

 25. I find that the plaintiffs examined- 4 witnesses including a son of original plaintiff, Tayab Ali to prove their case on possession. It is true, there are two statements in the deposition of PW 1 Alfaz Ali, a son of the original plaintiff, Tayeb Ali as recorded which are " আমার বাবা কবলা মূলে দখল করে না"  and   পক্ষভূক্ত তিন নম্বর বিবাদীরা দখল করে” I also find that before the conclusion of his examination- in-chief, PW 1 categorically has denied the suggestions that they did not possess the land and that the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 possess the suit land. Moreover, PW 2 Probhat Chandra Das, who was an employee in the sherista of Kali Mohan Mukherjee proved that Kali Mohan purchased the suit lands in auction, obtained sale certificate and got possession. Then, they annulled the encumbrances by service of notice. He also testified that Kali Mohan transferred the suit lands to Afsar Ali Howlader and Mokter Ali Howlader by a registered sale deed dated 8-6-1962 and Tayeb Ali, original plaintiff purchased the suit lands from said Howladers and possessed. He also identified the signature of Kali Mohan. 

 29. It has already been stated above that the appe1late court did not consider any evidence at all. Rather, the appellate court rejected the application for amendment as irrelevant for consideration that as the mistake in recording the deposition of PW 1 as mentioned in the application was not raised before the trial court at the proper time. 

 30. In the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners deserve serious consideration. It is true, the parties are litigating since long after the institution of the suit on 28-12-1981. In exercise of the jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, I am afraid, I can decide the pertinent question whether there was any such mistake during recording the statement of PW 1 Alfaz Ali, and if the answer is in the positive, then whether the application of the plaintiffs for amendment of the plaint should be allowed or not. If the case is a fit case for remand then where to send The learned Advocate for the opposite party requests for remand to the appellate court, in view of the delay. 

 31. I have already found that the appellate court did not consider any evidence on record nor gave its own decision on the question of title and possession. Moreover, it is the trial court which, can effectively dispose of the application for amendment of the plaint. If the application is found to be fit to allow the plaintiffs to add the prayer for confirmation of possession on payment of proper court fees, then, it can also allow the defendants to file additional written statement, if they so desire. There may be a necessity for additional evidence to be adduced by the parties for determining the real question in controversy between the parties. 

 "The importance of considering the evidence independently cannot be over-emphasised and the appellate judgment must reflect such consideration but in the case of affirming of the findings of the trial court, the narration of the entire evidence and reiteration of the reasons given by the trial court are not essential but expressions of general agreement with those of the trial court and proving additional reasons, if any, are generally considered sufficient. Expression of general agreement with reasons given by the court decision of which is under appeal would ordinarily suffice. In case of reversal of a finding of fact, however, the consideration of the evidence of necessity, has to be thorough and more elaborate. This case has no manner of application to the facts of the case. Rather, here, the judgment of the appellate court is based on total non-consideration of the evidence on record and absence of any finding of its own. In view of provisions of Order XLI rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure, such judgment must be held to be no judgment at all in the eye of law." 

 33. In the case of Abdul Mannan and others vs Akram Ali and others, 43 DLR (AD) 125, the suit for deciaration of title on the basis of settlement from the landlords was dismissed by the trial court but on appeal the appellate court allowed the appeal and decreed the suit finding the title and possession of the plaintiffs. In revision therefrom, this Division set aside the judgment of the appellate court and sent back the suit to the trial court on remand being of the view that finding of title of the plaintiff by the appellate court was based on misreading of the evidence on record particularly, the rent receipts. In further appeal, the Appellate Division allowed the appeal and set aside the impugned judgment and directed this Division to dispose of the revision applications on merit on the joint prayer of the learned Counsels on the ground that the entire evidence, both oral and documentary, was available on record and there was no necessity for remand. This case also does not support the opposite party.

lawyer:
M. Nurullah, Advocate, instructed by S.M. Huq, Advocate-on-Record------------For the Appellant. 
Md. Fazlul Karim, Advocate instructed by A. W. Mian. Advocate-on-Record----------For the Respondent.
parties:
Golam Hafez Mia. -------- Appellant.
Vs.
Khadem Ali Meah -------Respondent
full_judgment:
Facts material for the appeal are that dispute between plaintiff-appellant, Golan Hafez Mia, and defendant respondent, Khadem Ali Meah centres round the land belonging to Nalini and his wife Sarala. They left the country for West Bengal in 1962. Their rayati holding fell in arrears of rent which prompted the Government Acquired Estate to start four certificate proceedings. They are certificate case Nos. 138/1961-62, 185/1961-62, 187/1961-62, and 1970/1962-63. The holding comprising 1.72 acres of land was sold on 22-19-1962. It was purchased by the plaintiff, and he took delivery of possession on 4-10-62, Dispute between two parties cropped up when plain-tiff who had mututed his name in the Government Acquired Estate, found that the defendant on the basis of an ex-parte decree in Title Suit No. 730/62, had got his name entered in the record of rights. Defendant got the ex-party decree, as his name was omitted from the record of rights. His claim is that in Baishak 1350 B.S. corresponding to April 1973, he got settlement of the land from Nalini and Sarala, on the basis of Lakhik and has been in possession since then. The suit of the plaintiff was for declaration only. The suit was contested on various grounds; one was that the plaintiff did not acquire a valid title in the certificate sale, and the other was that he was not in possession of the property. 

 12. A certificate sale held in default of payment of rent, and on the compliance with the requirement of the principles of representation of the landlord and the tenant, the tenure or holding passes with the certificate sale. It has the effect of a rent decree. If the doctrine of representation is not fulfilled, it will have the effect of money decree. The consequence of a rent decree, is different from that of a money decree. The purchaser acquires a right in the property adversely to the right of the certificate debtor. He gets a paramount title, which extinguishes the rights of the certificate debtor, or any one claiming through him, subject to some interests described in the proviso to sub-section (3) of section 20. The purchaser, of course, has the right to annul all encumbrances mentioned in the sub-section. 

 24. In the result the appeal is allowed. with the above finding, the decisions of the courts below are set aside in part, and the case remitted back to trial Court for allowing the plaintiff- appellant to amend his pleading, by adding the prayer for recovery of possession on payment of proper court fees. The defendant shall be at liberty to file additional written statement, the court below shall decide the question of the recovery of possession by the plaintiff, and the ancillary question of adverse possession of the defendant, if so raised. The question will be decided on the evidence on record. The court shall, however, be at liberty to allow such additional evidence, if the parties pray and the court thinks fit to allow. The prayer for amendment if not made within three weeks of the arrival of the records in the court below, the shall be dismissed with cost. The cost of this appeal shall abide the result of the suit.

lawyer:
Qumrul Haque Siddique with Md. Abul Kalam Patowary and SM Harmuz Ahmed, Advocates -----For the petitioner and Respondent Nos. 6-11. 
Khair Ezaz Masud with Md. Mominullah Patwary Advocates -----For the Respondent No. 5.
parties:
Jahangir Maji ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Succinctly, the facts of the case, as stated in the writ petition, are that three groups of people, claiming themselves as the owners of the three different pieces of land, mutated their respective lands vide three Mutation cases namely, Mutation Case No. 4191 of 2011-2012 dated 15-3-2012, Mutation Case No. 5825 of 2011-2012 dated 11-6-2012 and Mutation Case no. 5824 of 2011-2012 dated 11-6-2012. While the writ petitioner's right, interest and claim, conjointly with that of respondent Nos. 8-10, lies in Mutation Case No. 5825 of 2011-2012, Mutation Case No. 5824 of 2011-2012 is with regard to the record of right of respondent Nos. 6 & 7 and Mutation Case No. 4191 deals with the record of right of respondent No.11. After coming to know about the above records of rights in the names of the above three sets of people, respondent No. 5 together with other two persons complained to the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Chandpur (hereinafter referred to as the A/C Land) on 17-1-2013 that the names of the petitioner and respondent nos. 6-11 (for ease of reference the petitioner and respondent nos. 6-11 hereinafter would be treated as one group and referred to as "the petitioners", given that their interest is same and they seek the same remedy) have been wrongly mutated and thus, prayed for reviewing the order passed by him in the aforesaid mutation cases. Pursuant to the said objection, the above three Mutation Cases were reheard upon being registered as Review Case No. 154 of 2012-2013 and by order dated 10-6- 2013 the A/C Land upon hearing both the sides cancelled the earlier mutations recorded in the names of the petitioners. The above U-turn stance of the A/C Land in disposing of the Review Case No. 154 of 2012-2013 prompted the petitioners to prefer an appeal before the appellate authority namely, Collector of Chandpur (respondent No.2) who allocated the same for disposal by respondent No. 3 who upon hearing both the parties allowed the appeal vide order dated 13-8- 2013. Against the said order dated 13-28-2013 respondent no.5 filed an application before respondent No.2 who asked respondent no. 3 to deal with the matter. Then, pursuant to an order passed by respondent No. 3 on 1-9-2013 the impugned order has been issued by the Officer-in- Charge of the office of respondent No. 2 and, hence, this Rule. 

 3. Respondent No.5 contested the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition contending, inter-alia, that the properties in question are owned and possessed by him and recording of the names of the petitioners thereon by the A/C Land was erroneous and, thus, respondent no.5 had to approach the A/C Land with supportive papers detailing the true position as to the title and possession of the lands and prayed to him for undertaking a review exercise of his own order in order to arrive at a correct decision in recording the names on the lands. The A/C Land having been briefed about the up-to-date position regarding the title and possession of the lands rightly cancelled the mutations of the petitioners in presence of both the sides. It is alleged that against the said review decision when the petitioners appealed before respondent No.3, the latter set aside the A/C Land's decision passed in the aforesaid Review Case by adopting fraudulent means and, under the circumstances, he had no other option but to approach respondent No. 2 with a prayer for investigation into the matter and, thereby, rehear the appeal in presence of both the sides. It is claimed by respondent No.5 that his approach before respondent No.2 is not made invoking the latter's jurisdiction of appeal or revision, rather it is an application for review of the order passed by respondent No.3. 

 (4) The Board of Land Administration may at any time order the correction of any entry in a record-of-rights maintained under this Part or in a settlement rent-roll prepared and finally published under this Part which, it is satisfied, has been made owing to a bona fide mistake: 

 (iv) The Board of Land Administration, however, shall be competent to order the correction of any entry at any time in presence of all the claimants of the land, if it finds any bona fide mistake in a finally published record-of-rights or in a settlement rent-roll.
